questions.prompt:
This text is adapted from the GED Study Guide.
DIRECTIONS: Read the text and choose the best answer to the question.
Petition: Ban Drilling for Resources in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge
To: U.S. Congress
We are urging members of the U.S. Congress to protect the nearly 9 million acres of unspoiled coastal plain and mountains in Alaska’s Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR). For many years, this land has been protected, but recently there has been a renewed call for accessing the oil in the Alaskan wilderness to boost the national economy and increase security. Today, more than 80% of Alaska’s state revenues result from the oil and gas business, a direct effect of tapping into Alaska’s rich energy reserves. Once again, economic interests in oil drilling and production of natural gas and coal are vying with environmental concerns, and the ANWR is in danger. The damage that could be done to the ecosystem would simply be too great.
QUESTION: What does the word revenues mean in the above text?
questions.explanation:
Answer:
c) income
Explanation:
Ask yourself the following questions, when trying to figure out the best answer:
What is the text about? It’s about protecting the environment in the face of economic and political pressure to exploit land for oil and gas.
Understand the question – what do you need to find? The meaning of the word revenues.
Find the key information – which sentence is the word revenues in? Today, more than 80% of Alaska’s state revenues result from the oil and gas business, a direct effect of tapping into Alaska’s rich energy reserves.
Can you predict the answer? In what way is the state of Alaska benefiting from oil and gas? Looking at the text around the key sentence, we learn that money and energy are the reasons that people want to drill for oil in ANWR. Both money and energy would make sense in place of the word revenues.
Do money and energy fit with any of the answers?
Energy doesn’t fit with any of the answers, but money fits with income. So,
income
is the best answer.

options.label: A
options.body: protection

options.label: B
options.body: lands

options.label: C
options.body: income

options.label: D
options.body: dangers

questions.prompt:
DIRECTIONS: Use this passage from
The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
by Mark Twain to answer the following question.
Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. … The retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash [paint]. By the time Ben was fagged [cigarettes] out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when
he
played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with – and so on, and so on, hour after hour. And when the middle of the afternoon came, from being a poor poverty-stricken boy in the morning, Tom was literally rolling in wealth.
QUESTION: In the text, the word
alacrity
means which of the following:
questions.explanation:
Answer:
b) readiness
Explanation:
Tom had reluctance (not wanting to do something) in his face,
but
alacrity in his heart. The word
but
helps the reader know that he feels differently in his heart than in his face. In the text, Tom relaxes and eats while he lets the other boys do his work if they give him treats. It seems like Tom has found a way to trick the other boys into doing his work for him.
He wasn’t sad, tired, or angry – he was secretly
ready
to give up the brush.

options.body: sadness

options.body: readiness

questions.prompt:
Adapted from TASC reading test practice items
DIRECTIONS: Read the text and then answer the question.
How to Shop Safely Online
What is the best way to save parking charges and avoid crowds at the mall? You can shop online. More and more consumers are finding online shopping the most convenient way to make purchases. In 2010, online sales on the day after Thanksgiving were 15.9 percent higher than they were in 2009. New technology even makes it possible to shop from mobile devices. However, there is a downside to this new and easy shopping access. Not every online site is safe from hackers, and some sites deliberately try to mislead consumers.
Some websites use web addresses that are formatted to look almost the same as legitimate sites. This tactic is called spoofing. The site may also use icons and trademarks similar to those on safe sites. A spoofed website often engages in another illegitimate activity called phishing. The object of phishing is to obtain credit card, bank account, or Social Security numbers from an unsuspecting consumer. On one of these sites, you might believe you are charging a pair of hiking boots, when you are actually providing some stranger with the information needed to book a flight to Acapulco on your credit card.
QUESTION: What does the word
legitimate
mean as it is used in the text?
questions.explanation:
Answer:
d) genuine
Explanation:
The clue is in the rest of the sentence: Some websites use web addresses that are formatted to look almost the same as legitimate sites. The text is about fake websites, and this sentence they make themselves look the same as … what is your prediction? They are trying to make themselves look real. Which of the answers fits best with real?
Only genuine means the same as real, so that is the correct answer.

options.label: A
options.body: accurate

options.label: B
options.body: believable

options.label: C
options.body: working

options.label: D
options.body: genuine

courses.content:
In this lesson… You will learn What is vocabulary? How can you figure out the meaning of a word? What are the steps to answering a vocabulary question?

Words to know Passage — section of text or quote from a book or other written material

Text — writing on a page or a digital screen

Vocabulary — set of words you know or use

Context clues — hints that can help you understand new words when you read a sentence or paragraph

Root word — A basic word to which affixes (prefixes and suffixes) are added

Prefix — word added to the beginning of a word

Suffix — a word added to the end of a word

What is Vocabulary? The language arts test will have many questions about pieces of text . One type of question is about the meaning of words. We call these types of questions vocabulary questions. Vocabulary means the words in a language. Your vocabulary is all the words you know. The test may ask you to figure out the meaning of just one word from the way it is used. It may be a word you already know, but it is being used in a different way. Or it may be a word you have not seen before. How can you figure out the meaning of a word? You can use context clues to find the meaning of the word by using the words and sentences around it.

Caption: It was an idyllic day ; sunny, warm and perfect for a walk in the park

In this picture we are trying to figure out the meaning of the word idyllic . If we look at the words around it like sunny, warm and perfect we can see that the author is saying the idyllic means perfect or just right.

Video: Context Clues Watch the video and then answer the practice questions.

Question 1 Read the following passage. Determine the meaning of the word Identical. “Mark Twain’s book “The Prince and the Pauper” is about two boys who look identical. One is a prince and one is a pauper. After they meet, they switch places with each other. They become trapped in the other boy’s world. Both boys have difficulty living as the other boy.” Question: In this passage, the word identical means which of the Question 1 Read the following text. Then answer the question. “Starting at age 55, our hippocampus, a brain region critical to memory, shrinks 1 to 2 percent every year, to say nothing of the fact that one in nine people age 65 and older has Alzheimer’s disease. The number afflicted is expected to grow rapidly as the baby boom generation ages. Given these grim statistics, it’s no wonder that Americans are a captive market for anything, from supposed smart drugs and supplements to brain training, which promises to boost normal mental functioning or to stem its all-too-common decline.” (courtesy of The New York Times.) QUESTION: In GED Exam Tip Exam tip What can you do to figure out the meaning of an unknown word? By now you should be able to figure out the meaning of an unknown word based on the meaning of the other words in the text. On your GED test, you may be asked to figure out the meaning of a word from the way it is used in the given text. It may be a word you already know, being used in a different way. Or it may be a word you have not seen before.

Video: Finding the Meaning of a Word Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

Video Transcript + Read the following passage. Determine the meaning of the word Identical. “Mark Twain’s book “The Prince and the Pauper” is about two boys who look identical. One is a prince and one is a pauper.

After they meet, they switch places with each other. They become trapped in the other boy’s world. Both boys have difficulty living as the other boy.” Question: In this passage, the word identical means which of the following? different Looking the same Brothers like a prince and pauper To answer a vocabulary question, there are six steps that you need to keep in your mind. The first three steps are questions you ask yourself to understand the text. While the other three help you arrive at the meaning. Step 1: Read the first sentence or two. This will give you an idea of the topic or theme. If it’s a short text like this one, you can read the whole thing quickly. The first sentence tells the reader about the plot of a book. The next sentences give more details about the story. Step 2: Read the directions and the question, but not the answers yet. For this question, you are looking for the meaning of the word identical. Step 3: Read the whole text and the answer choices. This step will help you understand which parts of the text are most important when figuring out the answer. Step 4: Find the key (important) information in the text. In this example, the key information is the word identical and the words around it that help us determine its meaning. Re-read the sentence that uses the word identical. Step 5: Try to predict the best answer. The two boys look identical and switch places with each other. These words tell us that the two boys are able to switch places because they look the same. Step 6: Choose the answer that is the best match for your predicted answer. A) “different” is not the best answer because there are no clues in the passage that they look different. It would be hard to switch places with someone if you looked different. B) “the same” is a good answer. It makes sense for the passage. We need to review the other options to make sure it is the best answer. C) “brothers” is not the best answer. Brothers would probably not be a prince and a pauper. Those are very different people in a community. D) “like a prince and a pauper” is a trick answer. The information is true: the boys are a prince and a pauper. But the word identical does not tell the reader that.

GED Exam Tip Exam tip When taking the GED, it is not necessary to understand every word in a text. It is more important to make sure you know what the question is asking you. If you do not understand a word, just keep reading. That word might not matter for answering the question. Instead, focus on understanding the question. In many questions on your GED or HiSET exam, you are being tested on your comprehension. Comprehension means how well you understand something. In your exam, understanding the question may be the most important part. In some cases, the answer will be obvious once you know what the question is asking.

Vocabulary review Passage — section of text or quote from a book or other written material

Text — writing on a page

Vocabulary — set of words you know or use

Context clues — hints that can help you understand new words when you read a sentence or paragraph

Root word — a basic word to which affixes (prefixes and suffixes) are added

Prefix — word added to the beginning of a word

Suffix — a word added to the end of a word

Summary Explore further: Discover additional resources to deepen your understanding. Root Words: Root words are the basic part of a word that gives it its main meaning. Other parts, like prefixes (beginnings) or suffixes (endings), can be added to root words to create new words. Here are some examples: Root Word: "act" Meaning: To do Examples: Action: The process of doing something. Actor: A person who performs in plays or movies. Root Word: "graph" Meaning: To write or draw Examples: Autograph: A person's own signature.

Photograph: A picture made using a camera. Root Word: "tele" Meaning: Far Examples: Telephone: A device to talk to someone far away. Television: A device to watch shows and movies broadcast from far away. Root Word: "bio" Meaning: Life Examples: Biology: The study of living things. Biography: The story of a person's life. Understanding root words can help you figure out the meaning of new words when you see them. Click here to see a list of Root Words from Greek and Latin languages.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker know it is winter in the first example?
questions.explanation:
Answer:
a) The character talks about building a snow fort.
Explanation:
The speaker infers that it is winter based on the character’s mention of building a snow fort. Building a snow fort is typically associated with winter activities, indicating the season.

options.label: A
options.body: The character talks about building a snow fort.

options.label: B
options.body: The character mentions enjoying hot chocolate.

options.label: C
options.body: The speaker has personal experience with winter activities.

options.label: D
options.body: The character is wearing warm clothing.

questions.prompt: Why do we make inferences when we read?
questions.explanation:
Answer
:
d) To understand the text by finding clues.
Explanation
:
We make inferences to understand the text better by finding and connecting clues within the writing. Inferences help us draw conclusions and fill in gaps that may not be explicitly mentioned.

options.label: A
options.body: To randomly guess about the text.

options.label: B
options.body: To notice details stated directly in the text.

options.label: C
options.body: To reach conclusions based on personal opinions.

options.label: D
options.body: To understand the text by finding clues.

questions.prompt: According to the video, how is an inference different from a guess?
questions.explanation:
Answer
:
c) An inference is supported by clues in the text, while a guess is a random assumption.
Explanation
:
An inference is different from a guess because it is based on clues found within the text, whereas a guess is a random assumption that may not have any evidence or support. Inferences are logical deductions drawn from the information provided in the writing.

options.label: A
options.body: An inference is based on personal opinion, while a guess is based on evidence.

options.label: B
options.body: An inference is a random guess, while a guess is a logical conclusion.

options.label: C
options.body: An inference is supported by clues in the text, while a guess is a random assumption.

options.label: D
options.body: An inference is a direct observation, while a guess is an educated deduction.

questions.prompt:
DIRECTIONS: Read the passage and answer the following question.
Passage from
To Kill a Mockingbird
by Harper Lee
Atticus was feeble: he was nearly fifty. When Jem and I asked him why he was so old, he said he got started late, which we felt reflected upon his abilities and manliness. He was much older than the parents of our school contemporaries, and there was nothing Jem or I could say about him when our classmates said, ‘My father – ’
Jem was football crazy. Atticus was never too tired to play keep-away, but when Jem wanted to tackle him Atticus would say, ‘I’m too old for that, son.’
Our father didn’t do anything. He worked in an office, not in a drugstore. Atticus did not drive a dump-truck for the county, he was not the sheriff, he did not farm, work in a garage, or do anything that could possibly arouse the admiration of anyone.
Besides that, he wore glasses. He was nearly blind in his left eye, and said left eyes were the tribal curse of the Finches. Whenever he wanted to see something well, he turned his head and looked from his right eye.
He did not do the things our schoolmates’ fathers did; he never went hunting, he did not play poker or fish or drink or smoke. He sat in the living-room and read.
With these attributes, however, he would not remain as inconspicuous as we wished him to; that year, the school buzzed with talk about him defending Tom Robinson, none of which was complimentary. After my bout with Cecil Jacobs when I committed myself to a policy of cowardice, word got around that Scout Finch wouldn’t fight any more, her daddy wouldn’t let her. This was not entirely correct: I wouldn’t fight publicly for Atticus, but the family was private ground. I would fight anyone from a third cousin upwards tooth and nail. Francis Hancock, for example, knew that.’
QUESTION: Which of the following is NOT something the narrator feels about her father?
questions.explanation:
Answer:
b) She resents him because he is strict.
Explanation:
Look for evidence of each statement (clues) in the passage before choosing an answer. There is evidence that the writer thinks her father is old and inactive, and that she finds him embarrassing. But there is no evidence that she thinks he is strict.

options.label: A
options.body: She thinks he is old.

options.label: B
options.body: She resents him because he is strict.

options.label: C
options.body: She wishes he were more active.

options.label: D
options.body: She is embarrassed by him.

With these attributes, however, he would not remain as inconspicuous as we wished him to; that year, the school buzzed with talk about him defending Tom Robinson, none of which was complimentary. After my bout with Cecil Jacobs when I committed myself to a policy of cowardice, word got around that Scout Finch wouldn’t fight any more, her daddy wouldn’t let her. This was not entirely correct: I wouldn’t fight publicly for Atticus, but the family was private ground. I would fight anyone from a third cousin upwards tooth and nail. Francis Hancock, for example, knew that.
When he gave us our air-rifles Atticus wouldn’t teach us to shoot. Uncle Jack instructed us in the rudiments thereof; he said Atticus wasn’t interested in guns. Atticus said to Jem one day, ‘I’d rather you shot at tin cans in the back yard, but I know you’ll go after birds. Shoot all the bluejays you want, if you can hit ‘em, but remember it’s a sin to kill a mockingbird.’
That was the only time I heard Atticus say it was a sin to do something, and I asked Miss Maudie about it. ‘Your father’s right,’ she said. ‘Mockingbirds don’t do one thing but make music for us to enjoy. They don’t eat up people’s gardens, don’t nest in corncribs, they don’t do one thing but sing their hearts out for us. That’s why it’s a sin to kill a mockingbird.’
QUESTION: Which of the following is the best description of Atticus?
questions.explanation:
Answer:
a) Quiet and educated
Explanation:
The passage gives you clues about the characters and what they are like. Both parts of the description must be right. Let’s make a list and ask ourselves, are there clues for the following?
quiet = yes
educated = yes
dull = yes
unkind = no
energetic = no
genuine = yes
unique = yes
humorous = no
Only the first answer gets two “yes”s, so it is the correct answer.

options.label: A
options.body: Quiet and educated

options.label: B
options.body: Dull and unkind

options.label: C
options.body: Energetic and genuine

options.label: D
options.body: Unique and humorous

There are some common sense ways to recognize a spoofed site. Check the web address carefully to make sure the domain name is in bold type. Make sure there are no typographical errors in the name. Spoofers often use a name that is just a few letters different from a legitimate site. Pay careful attention to any warnings from your web browser saying that a site is potentially unsafe. Keep your browser updated so you have the latest available protection.

In this lesson… You will learn What is an inference? How do we use inference in everyday life? How do you analyze a text to find inferences by following the four main steps? Step 1: Quickly read the text so that you know the main idea Step 2: Read the question and the answer choices Step 3: Look for clues in the text Step 4: Choose the answer that makes the most sense with your notes How can taking notes help you find the right answer?

Words to know Analyze — To think deeply about or study something to understand what it is

Conclusion — The end of something, or the decisions you make at the end of thinking about something

Imply — To suggest or indirectly say

Infer — To make a conclusion about something from direct or indirect information

Inference — A conclusion or belief based on what you know or assume

Logic — A way of thinking based on reasoning and using facts

Partially — In part, not fully, not completely

What is Inference? What is Inferring?

Inferring means making a conclusion or belief based on what you know or can guess. It’s about understanding things that aren’t directly said.

Everyday Use of Inferring

We use this skill every day. We look at the world around us and use our experiences to understand new information.

Example of Inferring

Imagine you have a friend who is usually talkative and funny. One day, you see him being very quiet, yawning, and rubbing his eyes. You don’t need him to say, “I’m really tired!” You can guess he is tired just by looking at him. This is an example of inferring. You used what you already knew to come to a conclusion.

Practicing Inferences for Tests

You already have the skills to answer inference questions on tests. You just need to practice with the kinds of texts you might see in the reading section. Look closely at the text and think about what it means.

Finding Inferences Let’s take a look at an inference question.

Read the following passage:

"Maria was completely wet. Her clothes stuck to her body, and water was dripping from her hair. She had an umbrella, but it was broken and not helpful. She walked quickly down the street, searching for a place to find shelter."

Now, answer the question based on the passage:

What can you guess about the weather?

A. It was sunny and dry. B. It was raining heavily. C. It was windy and cold. D. It was snowing.

The correct answer is B) It was raining heavily. We can figure this out by using the clues in the passage. When we see that Maria is completely wet, with clothes sticking to her body and water dripping from her hair, we can infer that it was raining heavily.

How to Analyze Text Let’s look at another inference question.

First, read the following excerpt from “Little Women” by Louisa May Alcott

"Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents," grumbled Jo, lying on the rug.

"It's so dreadful to be poor!" sighed Meg, looking down at her old dress.

"I don't think it's fair for some girls to have plenty of pretty things, and other girls nothing at all," added little Amy, with an injured sniff.

"We've got Father and Mother, and each other," said Beth contentedly from her corner.

The four young faces on which the firelight shone brightened at the cheerful words, but darkened again as Jo said sadly, "We haven't got Father, and shall not have him for a long time." She didn't say "perhaps never," but each silently added it, thinking of Father far away, where the fighting was.

Nobody spoke for a minute; then Meg said in an altered tone, "You know the reason Mother proposed not having any presents this Christmas was because it is going to be a hard winter for everyone; and she thinks we ought not to spend money for pleasure, when our men are suffering so in the army. We can't do much, but we can make our little sacrifices, and ought to do it gladly. But I am afraid I don't." And Meg shook her head, as she thought regretfully of all the pretty things she wanted."

Now, answer the question:

Which of the girls has the most grateful attitude?

• Jo

• Meg

• Amy

• Beth

Step-by-Step Solution:

As with vocabulary questions, we can use steps to answer inference questions.

Step 1: Quickly read the text so that you know the main idea

You don’t have to remember details. We know that it’s Christmas time, but there won’t be any presents. The girls are poor and probably sisters. The author also mentions fighting and the army. That is the context of the passage. Now, we can read and answer the question.

Step 2: Read the question and the answer choices

Now you know what information to look for, you can look at the question and answer choices. You need to find information in the text that will tell you which girl has the most grateful attitude.

Step 3: Look for clues in the text

Look back at the text. What does it tell you about the girls? You can make a note about each girl’s attitudes by reading what she says.

There are other clues in the text other than what the girls say. The author also used words to describe how each girl spoke:

Jo – grumbled Meg – sighed Amy – with an injured sniff Beth – contentedly

If you know the meaning of these words, you can use them to help you answer the question.

What should you do if, for example, you don’t know what the word “grateful” means? This makes answering the question harder, but you can still make a good guess. You know that you are looking for one girl whose attitude is different from the others’ attitudes. Since Jo, Meg, and Amy all said negative things, the answer is most likely to be Beth, because she focused on something different.

Step 4: Choose the answer that makes the most sense with your notes

Now compare your notes to the question. Of the four girls, the only one who said something positive, or grateful, was Beth.

Beth is the best answer for the most grateful.

Infer vs. Imply Commonly Confused Words: infer / imply

The difference between the two is that imply refers to giving information, while infer refers to receiving information.

Imply

Imply means to strongly suggest the truth or existence of something that is not expressly stated.

The speaker, or someone who is giving information, may imply something.

Example :

Jason's scowl {$\binom{\textbf{implied}}{\text{suggested}}$} that he was unhappy with the job.

Infer

Infer means to deduce or conclude information from evidence and reasoning rather than from explicit statement of that information.

The listener, or someone who is receiving information, may infer something.

From the tone of your voice, I am {$\binom{\textbf{inferring}}{\text{concluding}}$} that you are angry

The following examples clearly show the difference between the two words:

What are you {$\binom{\textbf{implying}}{\text{suggesting}}$} by your remark?

What should I {$\binom{\textbf{infer}}{\text{conclude}}$} from your remark?

Activity: Match Examples with correct words

Example 1:

Situation: You wake up in the morning and see the ground outside is wet.

• Inference: You infer that it rained overnight because wet ground is often a result of rain.

Example 2:

Situation: Your friend is shivering and their teeth are chattering.

• Inference: You infer that your friend is cold because shivering and chattering teeth are common responses to being cold.

Example 3:

Situation: You see smoke rising from a distant hill.

• Inference: You infer that there might be a fire because smoke is often a sign of fire.

Example 4:

Situation: Your coworker is repeatedly checking their watch and gathering their belongings.

• Inference: You infer that your coworker is preparing to leave because checking the watch and gathering belongings are typical behaviors before leaving.

Example 5:

Situation: Your teacher is handing out review sheets before a test.

• Inference: You infer that there will be a test soon because handing out review sheets is often done in preparation for a test.

Imply

Example 1 :

Statement : "I can't believe how messy the kitchen is."

• Implication: The speaker might be implying that someone should clean up the kitchen without directly stating it.

Example 2 :

Statement: "It's getting late."

• Implication: The speaker might be implying that it's time to leave without explicitly saying so.

Example 3 :

Statement: "I saw Sarah with a bunch of flowers."

• Implication: The speaker might be implying that Sarah received flowers from someone without directly mentioning the giver.

Example 4 :

Statement: "We should probably start saving money."

• Implication: The speaker might be implying that there are financial concerns or goals that require saving without explicitly stating them.

Example 5 :

Statement: "You look tired."

• Implication: The speaker might be implying that the person should rest without directly suggesting it.

She was a large woman with a large purse that had everything in it but hammer and nails. It had a long strap, and she carried it slung across her shoulder. It was about eleven o’clock at night, and she was walking alone, when a boy ran up behind her and tried to snatch her purse. The strap broke with the single tug the boy gave it from behind. But the boy’s weight and the weight of the purse combined caused him to lose his balance so, instead of taking off full blast as he had hoped, the boy fell on his back on the sidewalk, and his legs flew up. the large woman simply turned around and kicked him right square in his blue-jeaned sitter. Then she reached down, picked the boy up by his shirt front, and shook him until his teeth rattled. After that the woman said, “Pick up my pocketbook, boy, and give it here.” She still held him. But she bent down enough to permit him to stoop and pick up her purse. Then she said, “Now ain’t you ashamed of yourself?” Firmly gripped by his shirt front, the boy said, “Yes’m.” The woman said, “What did you want to do it for?” The boy said, “I didn’t aim to.” She said, “You a lie!” By that time two or three people passed, stopped, turned to look, and some stood watching. “If I turn you loose, will you run?” asked the woman. “Yes’m,” said the boy. “Then I won’t turn you loose,” said the woman. She did not release him. “I’m very sorry, lady, I’m sorry,” whispered the boy. “Um-hum! And your face is dirty. I got a great mind to wash your face for you. Ain’t you got nobody home to tell you to wash your face?” “No’m,” said the boy. “Then it will get washed this evening,” said the large woman starting up the street, dragging the frightened boy behind her. He looked as if he were fourteen or fifteen, frail and willow-wild, in tennis shoes and blue jeans. The woman said, “You ought to be my son. I would teach you right from wrong. Least I can do right now is to wash your face. Are you hungry?” “No’m,” said the being dragged boy. “I just want you to turn me loose.” “Was I bothering you when I turned that corner?” asked the woman. “No’m.” “But you put yourself in contact with me,” said the woman. “If you think that that contact is not going to last awhile, you got another thought coming. When I get through with you, sir, you are going to remember Mrs. Luella Bates Washington Jones.” Sweat popped out on the boy’s face and he began to struggle. Mrs. Jones stopped, jerked him around in front of her, put a half-nelson about his neck, and continued to drag him up the street. When she got to her door, she dragged the boy inside, down a hall, and into a large kitchenette furnished room at the rear of the house. She switched on the light and left the door open. The boy could hear other roomers laughing and talking in the large house. Some of their doors were open, too, so he knew he and the woman were not alone. The woman still had him by the neck in the middle of her room. She said, “What is your name?” “Roger,” answered the boy. “Then, Roger, you go to that sink and wash your face,” said the woman, whereupon she turned him loose—at last. Roger looked at the door—looked at the woman—looked at the door—and went to the sink. Let the water run until it gets warm,” she said. “Here’s a clean towel.” “You gonna take me to jail?” asked the boy, bending over the sink. “Not with that face, I would not take you nowhere,” said the woman. “Here I am trying to get home to cook me a bite to eat and you snatch my pocketbook! Maybe, you ain’t been to your supper either, late as it be. Have you?” “There’s nobody home at my house,” said the boy. “Then we’ll eat,” said the woman, “I believe you’re hungry—or been hungry—to try to snatch my pocketbook.” “I wanted a pair of blue suede shoes,” said the boy. “Well, you didn’t have to snatch my pocketbook to get some suede shoes,” said Mrs. Luella Bates Washington Jones. “You could of asked me.”

It was about eleven o’clock at night, and she was walking alone, when a boy ran up behind her and tried to snatch her purse. The strap broke with the single tug the boy gave it from behind. But the boy’s weight and the weight of the purse combined caused him to lose his balance so, instead of taking off full blast as he had hoped, the boy fell on his back on the sidewalk, and his legs flew up. the large woman simply turned around and kicked him right

square in his blue-jeansed sitter. Then she reached down, picked the boy up by his shirt front, and shook him until his teeth rattled.

After that the woman said, “Pick up my pocketbook, boy, and give it here.” She still held him. But she bent down enough to permit him to stoop and pick up her purse. Then she said, “Now ain’t you ashamed of yourself?” Firmly gripped by his shirt front, the boy said, “Yes’m.”

The woman said, “What did you want to do it for?”

The boy said, “I didn’t aim to.”

She said, “You a lie!”

By that time two or three people passed, stopped, turned to look, and some stood watching.

“If I turn you loose, will you run?” asked the woman.

“Yes’m,” said the boy.

“Then I won’t turn you loose,” said the woman. She did not release him.

“I’m very sorry, lady, I’m sorry,” whispered the boy.

“Um-hum! And your face is dirty. I got a great mind to wash your face for you. Ain’t you got nobody home to tell you to wash your face?”

“No’m,” said the boy.

“Then it will get washed this evening,” said the large woman starting up the street, dragging the frightened boy behind her. He looked as if he were fourteen or fifteen, frail and willow-wild, in tennis shoes and blue jeans.

The woman said, “You ought to be my son. I would teach you right from wrong. Least I can do right now is to wash your face. Are you hungry?”

“No’m,” said the being dragged boy. “I just want you to turn me loose.”

“Was I bothering you when I turned that corner?” asked the woman.

“No’m.”

“But you put yourself in contact with me,” said the woman. “If you think that that contact is not going to last awhile, you got another thought coming. When I get through with you, sir, you are going to remember Mrs. Luella Bates Washington Jones.”

Sweat popped out on the boy’s face and he began to struggle. Mrs. Jones stopped, jerked him around in front of her, put a half-nelson about his neck, and continued to drag him up the street. When she got to her door, she dragged the boy inside, down a hall, and into a large kitchenette furnished room at the rear of the house. She switched on the light and left the door open. The boy could hear other roomers laughing and talking in the large house. Some of their doors were open, too, so he knew he and the woman were not alone. The woman still had him by the neck in the middle of her room.

She said, “What is your name?”

“Roger,” answered the boy.

“Then, Roger, you go to that sink and wash your face,” said the woman, whereupon she turned him loose—at last. Roger looked at the door—looked at the woman—looked at the door—and went to the sink. Let the water run until it gets warm,” she said. “Here’s a clean towel.”

“You gonna take me to jail?” asked the boy, bending over the sink.

“Not with that face, I would not take you nowhere,” said the woman. “Here I am trying to get home to cook me a bite to eat and you snatch my pocketbook! Maybe, you ain’t been to your supper either, late as it be. Have you?”

“There’s nobody home at my house,” said the boy.

“Then we’ll eat,” said the woman, “I believe you’re hungry—or been hungry—to try to snatch my pocket book.”

“I wanted a pair of blue suede shoes,” said the boy. “Well, you didn’t have to snatch my pocketbook to get some suede shoes,” said Mrs. Luella Bates Washington Jones. “You could of asked me.” “M’am?”

The water dripping from his face, the boy looked at her. There was a long pause. A very long pause. After he had dried his face and not knowing what else to do dried it again, the boy turned around, wondering what next. The door was open. He could make a dash for it down the hall. He could run, run, run, run, run! The woman was sitting on the day-bed. After a while she said, “I were young once and I wanted things I could not get.”

There was another long pause. The boy’s mouth opened. Then he frowned, but not knowing he frowned.

The woman said, “Um-hum! You thought I was going to say but, didn’t you? You thought I was going to say, but I didn’t snatch people’s pocketbooks. Well, I wasn’t going to say that.”

Pause. Silence.

“I have done things, too, which I would not tell you, son—neither tell God, if he didn’t already know. So you set down while I fix us something to eat. You might run that comb through your hair so you will look presentable.”

In another corner of the room behind a screen was a gas plate and an icebox. Mrs. Jones got up and went behind the screen. The woman did not watch the boy to see if he was going to run now, nor did she watch her purse which she left behind her on the day-bed. But the boy took care to sit on the far side of the room where he thought she could easily see him out of the corner of her eye, if she wanted to. He did not trust the woman not to trust him. And he did not want to be mistrusted now.

“Do you need somebody to go to the store,” asked the boy, “maybe to get some milk or something?”

“Don’t believe I do,” said the woman, “unless you just want sweet milk yourself. I was going to make cocoa out of this canned milk I got here.”

“That will be fine,” said the boy.

She heated some lima beans and ham she had in the icebox, made the cocoa, and set the table. The woman did not ask the boy anything about where he lived, or his folks, or anything else that would embarrass him. Instead, as they ate, she told him about her job in a hotel beauty-shop that stayed open late, what the work was like, and how all kinds of women came in and out, blondes, red-heads, and Spanish. Then she cut him a half of her ten-cent cake.

“Eat some more, son,” she said.

When they were finished eating she got up and said, “Now, here, take this ten dollars and buy yourself some blue suede shoes. And next time, do not make the mistake of latching onto my pocketbook nor nobody else’s—because shoes come by devilish like that will burn your feet. I got to get my rest now. But I wish you would behave yourself, son, from here on in.”

She led him down the hall to the front door and opened it. “Good-night! Behave yourself, boy!” she said, looking out into the street. The boy wanted to say something else other than “Thank you, m’am” to Mrs. Luella Bates Washington Jones, but he couldn’t do so as he turned at the barren stoop and looked back at the large woman in the door. He barely managed to say “Thank you” before she shut the door. And he never saw her again.

text so that you know the main idea You don’t have to remember details. You just want a picture of the main idea – in this case, what the story is about. We know that it is nighttime and a boy tries to steal a woman’s purse because he wants some shoes. However, she catches him, and he says he is sorry. She takes the boy to her house, makes him wash his face, asks him if he’s had supper, and tells him they’re going to eat. Step 2: Read the question and the answer choices Now you know what information to look for. In this question, you are looking for text that gives descriptions of Mrs. Jones’ character. Step 4: Choose the answer that makes the most sense with your notes The text tells us that Mrs. Jones is tough (she is not afraid of the boy and is even aggressive with him) but also compassionate (she takes him home to give him food), so the correct answer is (C). question. How to Shop Safely Online What is the best way to save parking charges and avoid crowds at the mall? You can shop online. More and more consumers are finding online shopping the most convenient way to make purchases. In 2010, online sales on the day after Thanksgiving were 15.9 percent higher than they were in 2009. New technology even makes it possible to shop from mobile devices. However, there is a downside to this new and easy shopping access. Not every online site is safe from hackers, and some sites deliberately try to mislead consumers. Some websites use web addresses that are formatted to look almost the same as legitimate sites. This tactic is called spoofing. The site may also use icons and trademarks similar to those on safe sites. A spoofed website often engages in another illegitimate activity called phishing. The object of phishing is to obtain credit card, bank account, or Social Security numbers from an unsuspecting consumer. On one of these sites, you might believe you are charging a pair of hiking boots, when you are actually providing some stranger with the information needed to book a flight to Acapulco on your credit card. questions.prompt:
Read the text below and answer the question.
Driverless cars zooming past cities’ preparations, report says
Detroit Free Press
,
adapted from newsela.com.
The technology industry is racing to create a self-driving vehicle and get it on the road in the next 10 years. To be successful, America’s urban planners need to resolve a host of questions. It is their job to determine how cities will respond to the future of transportation.
A new report finds only 6 percent of U.S. cities have
devoted
planning resources to figuring out changes needed to accommodate self-driving vehicles. Only 3 percent have studied the impact of taxi alternatives like Uber and Lyft.
However, 50 percent of cities’ plans recommend new highway construction. More roads, more lanes and more parking garages will help deal with traffic in the traditional way.
Among the questions that cities need to consider:
Will the arrival of self-driving vehicles require dedicated lanes for them?
Will autonomous vehicles reduce the need for downtown parking garages? One possible future would see most self-driving cars as part of large fleets operated by services like Uber and Lyft.
Should cities spend more on public transportation to help reduce dependence on privately owned cars?
“The rate of change is definitely happening much faster,” Rainwater said. “Cities are getting up to speed and they’re looking at what they can do.” Still, he said, the planning perspective often has not been aligning with how quickly technology has been changing.
QUESTION: Which of the following best states the main idea of the text?
questions.moduleTitle: Practice Quiz: Finding the Main Idea
questions.explanation:
Answer:
B)
There are many things city planners need to consider before self-driving vehicles become available, but so far they have been slow to do this.
Explanation:
Let us follow the same steps that we used before:
Step 1:
Quickly read the text.
Make a list (either on paper or in your mind) of ideas in the text.
The ideas in the text are:
self-driving vehicles/autonomous vehicles
urban planners
very few cities considering future of autonomous vehicles
half of cities thinking about traditional traffic solutions
many questions
self-driving vehicles from services such as Uber and Lyft
city planning not quick enough for technology
Step 2:
Read the question and the answer choices.
Then read the text a second time if you need to.
Evaluate each answer, one at a time. Remind yourself each time that the question is asking about the main idea or point of the text.
A. Self-driving vehicles still require much testing and development before they can be introduced to consumers.
This answer is incorrect because, while the text does mention the development of autonomous vehicles, it also talks at great length about what city planners need to do to anticipate them. The article’s paragraphs do not focus on the testing and development of self-driving vehicles.
B. There are many things city planners need to consider before self-driving vehicles become available, but so far they have been slow to do this.
This answer could be the best answer option. The article talks a lot about what urban planners need to be thinking about. The author mentions several times that cities are not thinking enough about the future of autonomous vehicles.
First paragraph:  “America’s urban planners need to resolve a host of questions.”
Second paragraph: “… only 6 percent of U.S. cities have devoted planning resources to figuring out changes needed to accommodate self-driving vehicles.”
Last paragraph: “… the planning perspective often has not been aligning with how quickly technology has been changing.”
This seems like a good answer. Read through and evaluate the last two options to confirm that B is the main idea.
C. In the future, public transportation and self-driving vehicles will help cut down on traffic in cities.
The article mentions public transportation and traffic, but this answer has nothing specific about self-driving vehicles. This is not the best answer.
D. Services such as Uber and Lyft are leading the way in developing self-driving vehicles.
Uber and Lyft are mentioned in the article. However, the article never says that they are developing autonomous vehicles.  This answer does not say anything about city planning.
After reading and evaluating all four options, we find that B is the best answer.

options.body: Self-driving vehicles still require much testing and development before they can be introduced to consumers.

options.label: B
options.body: There are many things city planners need to consider before self-driving vehicles become available, but so far they have been slow to do this.

options.label: C
options.body: In the future, public transportation and self-driving vehicles will help cut down on traffic in cities.

options.label: D
options.body: Services such as Uber and Lyft are leading the way in developing self-driving vehicles.

questions.prompt:
Please read this passage and answer the following question.
Source of Passage:
Newsla.Com
Smoking in China
Every day in China, women go to work in smoke-filled offices, exposed to the fumes of cigarettes smoked mainly by male colleagues. After work is over, many go home to breathe secondhand
smoke created by husbands or other family members.
According to the most recent national survey, 288 million men smoked regularly in China in 2010, compared with 13 million women. Lately, the women are striking back. Last fall, China’s State Council proposed the nation’s toughest restrictions yet on indoor smoking and the marketing of tobacco. The announcement was a major victory for China’s tobacco-control movement, which includes several women who’ve been on the front lines for decades.
China’s anti-smoking movement also includes many prominent men. Former NBA center Yao Ming and other celebrities have lent their names to the cause. Yet in government and among tobacco-control groups, women are leading the charge. China’s health commissioner, Li Bin, has been outspoken in seeking a national indoor-smoking ban. Li sits on the State Council, a top-level panel that drafted the restrictions unveiled in November. Two of her key deputies are women.
The battle is far from won. Although smoking rates have declined in recent years, more than half of Chinese men smoke regularly, according to the WHO. Some 700 million Chinese — twice the population of the United States — are routinely exposed to secondhand smoke, which kills an estimated 100,000 people annually.
Chinese have smoked tobacco for centuries, and up until the early 1900s women regularly could be seen with men puffing on pipes. But with the advent of cigarettes, Chinese intellectuals and foreign missionaries started frowning on women who smoked.  As a result, women quit smoking, even as Chinese leaders such as Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping smoked openly in public, encouraging the habit among men.
QUESTION: Which of the following statements contains the main ideas of the article?
questions.explanation:
Answer: b
) Women are at the head of the anti-smoking movement in China, and they are fighting against years of tradition.
Explanation:
The statement that contains the main ideas of the article is: b) Women are at the head of the anti-smoking movement in China, and they are fighting against years of tradition
This answer captures the article’s focus on the role of women leading the charge against smoking, the health risks they face, and their efforts to challenge long-standing smoking habits in Chinese society.

options.label: A
options.body: Women are at the head of the anti-smoking movement in China, and they are fighting against years of tradition.

options.label: B
options.body: China's government has a monopoly on the country's tobacco industry.

options.label: C
options.body: Secondhand smoke affects more women than men in China.

options.label: D
options.body: China is making strides in making smoking less popular.

questions.prompt:
Please read this text to answer the question.
Source:
Newsla.Com
Concussion among teenagers
New research finds that after sustaining a mild brain injury, such as a concussion from playing sports, nearly 9 in 10 teens who have ongoing symptoms also have academic problems related to headaches, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating. More than three-quarters of those who have yet to recover fully after four weeks report a decline in academic skills. A new study shows the consequences of some brain injuries can extend well beyond the playing field and can persistently hurt an adolescent’s academic performance in and outside the classroom.
Among 349 students ages 5 to 18 who had suffered a concussion, 240 continued to experience physical and cognitive symptoms of brain injury, including headaches, dizziness, light sensitivity, and problems of mood and concentration within four weeks of their injury. In that group, those with the highest academic demands — generally students in middle and high school — were most likely to report persistent symptoms of concussions along with difficulties concentrating and keeping up with schoolwork, especially math.
For most with mild brain injuries, the process of recovery will take one to three weeks. During that time, physicians have suggested limiting school time, lessening the amount of homework, and including frequent breaks throughout the day. Administrators might allow a concussed student to move between classes ahead of the noise and confusion after the bell, to reschedule tests, and to let a student eat lunch in a quiet place.
QUESTION: What is a concussion?

a) A mild brain injury
Explanation:
We know a concussion is a
mild brain injury
from the passage because it explicitly states, “after sustaining a mild brain injury, such as a concussion from playing sports.” This directly defines a concussion as a type of mild brain injury.

options.body: A mild brain injury

options.label: B
options.body: A player in a sport

How Shall Employees Conduct Themselves?
Guidelines for Conducting Business with Those Outside Our Company
Our employees are the most effective advertisement of our values, beliefs, and abilities. Always keep in mind that when you are acting in your capacity as our employee, you are contributing materially to the public image and the ultimate success of this company.
Gifts for Influence
No payment or gift of money, goods, or services should be given or received to influence government or business decisions. Accurate and complete records for all accounts will be strictly monitored for everyone’s protection. If it becomes apparent to you in the course of the performance of your business responsibilities that a payment of some kind is expected by your business associate, please contact your division president.
Conflict of Interest
A conflict of interest can be described as a situation where a person has a vested interest in two areas of the business world that may give him or her an unfair advantage in business dealings. Our employees should be sensitive to any relationship that creates such a relationship—or even creates the appearance of such a relationship.
Keep these rules in mind
:
• Throughout your employment period, be vigilant about potential conflicts of interest between this company’s interests and your personal or immediate family’s interests.
• Don’t use your position with this company to obtain a personal benefit of any kind.
• Avoid any action or relationship that creates, or even creates the appearance of, a conflict of interest. For example, having an interest in a nonpublic company that competes or does business with our company or any of its affiliates might create the appearance of a conflict of interest and might prompt accusations and/or an investigation.
Disclosure
This company respects your privacy, as well as your right to conduct your personal affairs without interference; however, you must make prompt, complete, and continuing disclosure of all facts relating to any factual or potential conflict of interest.
Investigations
Inquiries or investigations may be undertaken at this company’s direction by its attorneys, investigators, internal auditors, or independent public accountants. Employees should regard this vigilance as the company’s commitment not only to fair competition but also to the protection of its employees. Your cooperation is needed for your protection as well as that of this company, and it is a condition of your employment.

courses.content:
In this lesson… You will learn What is the main idea of a text? Which test questions are about the main idea? What questions should you ask yourself to find the main idea? What are the steps for finding the main idea?

Words to know Detail — small fact or part of something bigger

Statement — clear expression or announcement

Summarize — give the main ideas or points of something

Theme — idea, thread, or tone running through a piece of writing, a work of art, or an event

Main idea — the central idea of a text

The Main Idea Imagine that someone shows you the picture below and asks,

“What is this a photo of? Tell me in just a few words.”

Which answer would be the best?

• “It’s a wedding.”

• “They’re outside.”

• “The flowers are red and white.”

• “There are lots of people.”

• “It shows a man and woman.”

All of those things are true. But which answer tells you the main point? The main point is that a wedding is taking place. That is the most important thing in the picture – it is the main idea.

The passages of text you read in your test will have many details, but there will be one “big picture” idea that the author wants to make clear for the readers. It may be a topic, or it may be a theme . When you are asked for the main point of the text, remember the difference between details and big ideas!

How To Find the Main Idea All of the following questions are asking about the main idea:

• Which of the following best summarizes the main idea of the text?

• Which of the following sentences best summarizes the theme of the passage?

• Which of these statements best describes the theme of the text?

• Which of the following best states the main idea of the text?

• The topic of the passage is …

What should I ask myself to identify the main idea?

You can find answers to these questions by asking yourself, “What is this text about?” or “What is one important point the author wants me to know or remember?”

What are the steps for finding the main idea?

Sometimes, answering the simple questions above is not so easy. Let’s look at the steps we need to take to find the main idea if it is not immediately clear.

Here is our sample text – we made some important ideas bold to help you:

Changing the ecosystem

Text adapted from teacher.depaul.edu

A food chain is a series of links between plants and animals . It starts with a plant. The next part of the link is a plant eater. When the prairie plants started to die or were replaced with houses and roads , the animals that depended on them lost their food source. While farmers produced more food for people, they broke the animals’ food chain and the animals died or had to move . This was a great mistake. We are paying for that mistake today. And, unfortunately, people still keep making the mistake of breaking food chains .

A food chain is part of a bigger system called a food web. That web links the living things in an ecosystem. The herbivores in that system depend on the plants. If the plants are removed, the herbivores (animals which eat plants) cannot survive. Then the carnivores, the animals that eat other animals, lose their food, too. Remove just one kind of plant from an environment and you disrupt the food web. Plow up the land and you destroy the whole system . The problem was there were more and more people and less and less natural habitat .

By 1900, Illinois and other Midwestern states were becoming known as the nation’s breadbasket. This was because millions of acres of land had been turned from prairie into farms . Those farms could grow corn, wheat, and other grains. Those grains were used to make bread and other food for people. This was not progress for everyone. That agricultural progress benefited many people . The farmers and businesses that processed the grains prospered. Chicago’s population grew , and it became a center for transportation and industry, too. More and more homes, businesses, and roads were built. Many of the animals and plants that were native to this area were destroyed, as was the natural system called the prairie.

QUESTION : Which of the following best states the main idea of the text?

• The population of Chicago grew significantly.

• More farmland was needed to grow crops as the cities of the US expanded.

• When humans destroy the natural habitat of a plant or animal, it negatively affects many other species in the ecosystem.

• Special measures should be taken to protect the habitats of native plants and animals in the Midwest against city expansion and farming.

Let’s look at the video on the next page to help us answer.

Video: Finding Key Ideas Video Transcripts + Sometimes, finding the main idea in a GED Reading Language Arts test can be challenging. However, by following a few simple steps, you can improve your chances of success. Let's take a look at the steps you can take to find the main idea if it's not immediately clear. Consider the following question and answer choices: Based on the article you read , which of the following best states the main idea of the text? A. The population of Chicago grew significantly. B. More farmland was needed to grow crops as the cities of America expanded. C. When humans destroy the natural habitat of a plant or animal, it negatively affects many other species in the ecosystem. D. Special measures should be taken to protect the habitats of native plants and animals in the Midwest against city expansion and farming. Step 1 : Read the text quickly. You do not need to remember all of the details. You need to look for important themes or ideas. In our example above, we made some important ideas bold to help you. Make a list of these key ideas, either on paper or in your mind. Your list may say: food chain/food web growing population (Chicago) roads/farms changing the land animals die or move system destroyed humans benefit Step 2 : Read the question and the answer choices. Then read the text a second time if you need to. This type of question (which of the following best states the main idea of the text?) can be challenging. This is because more than one of these ideas appears in the text. You just have to figure out what the most important idea is. That will show you the best statement. To figure it out, you may need to consider each of the options, one at a time: Answer A: T he population of Chicago grew significantly. The text supports this conclusion. However, Chicago is not mentioned in the first or second paragraph, which is a clue that this is not the most important idea. So A is true but probably not the most important idea. Answer B: More farmland was needed to grow crops as the cities of America expanded. The author mentions the need for more farmland in the first and last paragraphs. However, the author only mentions the population growth of one city, Chicago. This answer option also does not include anything about the destruction of plants and animal habitats, something which was mentioned

throughout the text. Sometimes an answer choice will be wrong because it leaves out something important. B leaves out information about the food chain and animals. Answer C: When humans destroy the natural habitat of a plant or animal, it negatively affects many other species in the ecosystem. This includes ideas about both humans and plants/animals. The idea that people can harm plants and animals by changing the land comes up repeatedly and in different places in the text. For example: First paragraph: “While farmers produced more food for people, they broke the animals’ food chain and the animals died or had to move.” Second paragraph: “Plow up the land and you destroy the whole system.” Third paragraph: “Many of the animals and plants that were native to this area were destroyed, as was the natural system called the prairie.” This is the best answer so far. We will look at option D to make sure that it is not a better answer. Answer D: Special measures should be taken to protect the habitats of native plants and animals in the Midwest against city expansion and farming. In this case, measures means actions taken with a specific purpose. This option is proposing that specific actions be taken. This is a tempting answer because it mentions both natural habitats and human activity. However, the author did NOT make any suggestions about how to solve the problem. He wrote about the problems but did not discuss special measures. Avoid answers that are related but not in the text. After reading all four options, C seems to be the best option. The right answer is C. Click "Continue" to watch a video about finding the meaning of words from the context clues and surrounding words.

Video: What is a main idea? (no text content — video or interactive topic)

GED Exam Tip Exam tip The reading section on the GED® Language Arts exam uses questions that test how carefully you read. Multiple-choice questions, like those about the main idea, are all asking you to do one thing: find which of several statements are correct or incorrect. They might say, What is the main idea? or Choose the best answer or Which of these statements is NOT true? The best way to find the right answer is to test the possible answers against the text. When you follow the steps for finding the main idea, that is what you are doing. You can use this strategy for many other questions. Compare the answers one by one to the information you were given. Keep the question in mind each time. You will need to do this quickly in your test. With many of the answer choices, you will easily see they are wrong when you test them. But you should test them all, even if you think the first answer is the right one!

Vocabulary review Detail — small fact or part of something bigger

Statement — clear expression or announcement

Summarize — give the main ideas or points of something

Theme — idea, thread, or tone running through a piece of writing, a work of art, or an event

Main Idea — the central idea of a text.

Summary What we learned The main idea is the point of the text or its most important theme. Questions about the main idea use words such as theme, topic, and summarize. To identify the main idea, first ask yourself, "In a few words, what is the text about or what does the writer most want me to know?" To identify the main idea or ideas in a text: Read the text, make a list of ideas mentioned in the text, and then look at the answers one at a time. Find the one which contains the most important idea or ideas from your list.

Explore further: Discover additional resources to deepen your understanding. English: Click on this link to practice identifying the main idea and theme. Español: Haz clic en este enlace para practicar cómo identificar la idea principal y el tema.

in China Every day in China, women go to work in smoke-filled offices, exposed to the fumes of cigarettes smoked mainly by male colleagues. After work is over, many go home to breathe secondhand smoke created by husbands or other family members. According to the most recent national survey, 288 million men smoked regularly in China in 2010, compared with 13 million women. Lately, the women are striking back. Last fall, China’s State Council proposed the nation’s toughest restrictions yet on indoor smoking and the marketing of tobacco. The announcement was a major victory for China’s tobacco-control movement, which includes several women who’ve been on the front lines for decades. China’s anti-smoking movement also includes many prominent men. Former NBA center Yao Ming and other celebrities have lent their names to

the cause. Yet in government and among tobacco-control groups, women are leading the charge. China’s health commissioner, Li Bin, has been outspoken in seeking a national indoor-smoking ban. Li sits on the State Council, a top-level panel that drafted the restrictions unveiled in November. Two of her key deputies are women. The battle is far from won. Although smoking rates have declined in recent years, more than half of Chinese men smoke regularly, according to the WHO. Some 700 million Chinese — twice the population of the United States — are routinely exposed to secondhand smoke, which kills an estimated 100,000 people annually. Chinese have smoked tobacco for centuries, and up until the early 1900s women regularly could be seen with men puffing on pipes. But with the advent of cigarettes, Chinese intellectuals and foreign missionaries started frowning on women who smoked. As a result, women quit smoking, even as Chinese leaders such as Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping smoked openly in public, encouraging the habit among men. research finds that after sustaining a mild brain injury, such as a concussion from playing sports, nearly 9 in 10 teens who have ongoing symptoms also have academic problems related to headaches, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating. More than three-quarters of those who have yet to recover fully after four weeks report a decline in academic skills. A new study shows the consequences of some brain injuries can extend well beyond the playing field and can persistently hurt an adolescent’s academic performance in and outside the classroom. Among 349 students ages 5 to 18 who had suffered a concussion, 240 continued to experience physical and cognitive symptoms of brain injury, including headaches, dizziness, light sensitivity, and problems of mood and concentration within four weeks of their injury. In that group, those with the highest academic demands — generally students in middle and high school — were most likely to report persistent symptoms of concussions along with difficulties concentrating and keeping up with schoolwork, especially math. For most with mild brain injuries, the process of recovery will take one to three weeks. During that time, physicians have suggested limiting school time, lessening the amount of homework, and including frequent breaks throughout the day. Administrators might allow a concussed student to move between classes ahead of the noise and confusion after the bell, to reschedule tests, and to let a student eat lunch in a quiet place. QUESTION: What is a concussion? passage because it explicitly states, “after sustaining a mild brain injury, such as a concussion from playing sports.” This directly defines a concussion as a type of mild brain injury.

questions.prompt:
Please read the following article and then answer the question below.
The
Awe-inspiring Revelations of Astronauts
By Jessica Hullinger
Adapted from the week.com
1) Astronaut Kjell Lindgren spent close to five months on the International Space Station last year serving as a NASA flight engineer and mission specialist. He still remembers the first time he saw the Earth from space.
2) “I saw this really bright white light coming through the small windows…I took a peek and saw the beautiful blue and whites of the Earth below, and the curvature of the horizon. Getting to experience the whole disc of the Earth from that point of view, truly for me, it was this breathtaking experience. I got goosebumps.”
3) Humans have been going to space for five decades now, and during that time, numerous astronauts have returned from orbit with reports eerily similar to Lindgren’s. Theirs are tales of profound inspiration, overwhelming emotion, a sense of oneness, even transcendence.
4) “No amount of prior study or training can fully prepare anybody for the awe and wonder this inspires,” wrote space shuttle astronaut Kathryn D. Sullivan. It’s “one of the deepest, most emotional experiences I have ever had,” said NASA astronaut Gene Cernan. “You realize that on that small spot, that little blue and white thing, is everything that means anything to you,” said Apollo 9 astronaut Russell Schweickart. “All of history and music and poetry and art and death and birth and love, tears, joy, games, all of it on that little spot out there.”
5) In 1987, this phenomenon was given a name: the Overview Effect. Here’s how it’s defined by the Overview Institute: The Overview Effect is the experience of seeing firsthand the reality of the Earth in space, which is immediately understood to be a tiny, fragile ball of life, hanging in the void, shielded and nourished by a paper-thin atmosphere. From space, the astronauts tell us, national boundaries vanish, the conflicts that divide us become less important and the need to create a planetary society with the united will to protect this “pale blue dot” becomes both obvious and imperative.
6) Or, as Apollo 14 astronaut Edgar Mitchell perfectly and simply put it, “Something happens to you out there.” Indeed, for many astronauts, seeing the Earth from above does more than fill them with a fleeting sense of wonder. It changes them. Many devote their lives to religion or find a renewed sense of faith.
7) Despite its life-altering potential, the Overview Effect has never really been studied empirically. David Yaden wants to change that. He’s a research scientist at the University of Pennsylvania’s Positive Psychology Center, where he studies spiritual experiences through the lenses of psychology and neuroscience. He’s also the lead author on a new paper that examines what, exactly, the Overview Effect does to the mind, and how its powers could be harnessed to promote health.
8) His conclusion? The Overview Effect elicits a sense of awe in its purest, most intense form. Emotion researchers have only recently begun studying the effects of awe, but they believe we experience awe when we are confronted with something vast, either physically big (the Grand Canyon, for example) or conceptually huge (like meeting your favorite celebrity). For a moment, this vastness confuses the mind, and forces the brain to accommodate by making room for what it’s seeing.
9) “The Overview Effect seems to contain both of those aspects of awe,” Yaden told The Week. “You’re seeing an entire half of the planet all at once, which is vast beside the blackness of space. But on the conceptual side, Earth represents all we find meaningful as human beings. Many of the astronauts discuss this aspect as well, seeing the fragility and the beauty of the planet at once and having this epiphany or realization of how precious the planet is and how much we need to do more to protect it.”
10) Back on Earth, awe has been linked to pro-social behavior, altruism, and inclusive thinking. But it’s also been shown to have positive effects on everything from creativity to physical health. One study linked higher instances of wonder to lower levels of harmful, disease-linked inflammation markers, even more so than other positive emotions like love and joy.
11) Unfortunately, most of us will never have the privilege of going to space. How can we get a taste of the Overview Effect without leaving the confines of gravity? “We don’t need to go to space to benefit from intense experiences of awe,” Yaden says. “We can experience a little bit of the Overview Effect on mountain tops or by viewing a beautiful sunset. There are a lot of opportunities for these experiences that are all around us.” So put down the smartphone. Go outside and take in the view. Glance up at the stars and ponder your very existence on our own pale blue dot, and let the awe wash over you.
QUESTION: Which of the following sentences best summarizes the main idea of the article?
questions.explanation:
Answer:
b) The wonder that astronauts experience when they see Earth from space has many positive effects, and we can also enjoy these benefits by finding awe in our daily lives
Explanation:
The sentence that best summarizes the main idea of the article is:
“The wonder that astronauts experience when they see Earth from space has many positive effects, and we can also enjoy these benefits by finding awe in our daily lives.”
This captures the essence of the Overview Effect, its emotional impact on astronauts, and the suggestion that similar experiences of awe can be found on Earth.

options.label: A
options.body: Astronauts are fortunate to experience things that most people will never have the opportunity to do.

options.label: B
options.body: The wonder that astronauts experience when they see Earth from space has many positive effects, and we can also enjoy these benefits by finding awe in our daily lives.

options.label: C
options.body: People who see Earth from space are overwhelmed by emotion and later struggle to adjust to life back on Earth.

options.label: D
options.body: Studying the Overview Effect is difficult because there are so few people who have seen Earth from space, and each person's experience is unique.

questions.prompt:
Please read the following article and then answer the question below.
The World Has a Problem: Too Many Young People
By SOMINI SENGUPTA MARCH 5, 2016
Adapted from The New York Times
At no point in recorded history has our world been so demographically lopsided, with old people concentrated in rich countries and the young in not-so-rich countries.
Much has been made of the challenges of aging societies. But it’s the youth bulge that stands to put greater pressure on the global economy, encourage political unrest, cause mass migration and have significant consequences for everything from marriage to Internet access to the growth of cities. A fourth of humanity is now young (ages 10 to 24). The vast majority live in the developing world, according to the United Nations Population Fund.
Nowhere can the pressures of the youth bulge be felt as profoundly as in India. Every month, some one million young Indians turn 18 — coming of age, looking for work, registering to vote and making India home to the largest number of young, working-age people anywhere in the world.
Already, the number of Indians between the ages of 15 and 34 — 422 million — is roughly the same as the combined populations of the United States, Canada and Britain.
Worldwide, young workers are in a difficult situation. Two out of five are either not working or working in such ill-paid jobs that they can’t escape poverty, according to figures recently released by the International Labour Organization. In the developing world, where few can afford to be unemployed, most young workers have jobs that are unpredictable, poorly paid and offer no legal protection; women are worse off.
Youth unemployment is especially striking in richer countries. Across Europe, youth unemployment is 25 percent, not just because of a sluggish economy but because many young Europeans don’t have the skills for the jobs available, from electricians to home health aides. In the United States, nearly 17 percent of those between the ages of 16 and 29 are neither in school nor working.
That does not bode well. An increase in youth unemployment is a better predictor of social unrest than virtually any other factor, warned Raymond Torres, the Labour Organization’s research chief. “The social contract is weakened because of unfulfilled promises,” he said.
In some ways, the global demographic portrait reflects what we are doing right: Our babies are far less likely to die, and our grandparents live longer. Women have fewer
children, and die less often in childbirth. More good news: Primary school enrollment has increased in the developing world. In India, for instance, nearly all children are enrolled in school.
But even those gains are uneven. According to the latest survey carried out by a national nonprofit called Pratham, half of Indian schoolchildren enrolled in fifth grade are unable to read from a second-grade textbook, and half cannot subtract. They’re in school, but they are not learning much.
What’s more, even modest education fuels ambition. Yet it can also frustrate those who can’t find work. Across the Middle East, where authoritarian rulers invested in education, youth unemployment is soaring — along with unrest.
The global generation gap is widening. In Germany, the median age is over 46, and in Russia, 39. In the United States, the median age is over 37; in India, 27; and in Nigeria, just over 18. China is running out of young workers so fast that it ended its decades-old one-child policy last year to allow married couples to have two children.
The worldwide age divide makes migration and job creation critical to balancing the world demographically, according to Rainer Münz, head of research and development at the Erste Group Bank in Brussels. Mr. Münz proposes what he calls a system in which industrialized countries compete for talent from elsewhere. Even China, he maintains, will have to enter that race.
“An exchange between aging societies with a shrinking work force and youthful societies would be a good thing, if the whole thing could be managed,” he said.

c) Youth in many countries around the world are struggling to find adequate employment.

The best summary of the main ideas of the article is:
Youth in many countries around the world are struggling to find adequate employment.
This option captures the central focus of the article, which discusses the challenges faced by young people, particularly in developing countries, regarding employment and the broader implications of the global youth bulge.
