In this lesson… You will learn What are capital letters? What are proper nouns and why are they capitalized? What are other uses for capital letters? What is a good rule to use for capital letters in essays?

Words to know Acronym — set of letters (usually the first letter in a string of words) used as a name of something, such as a company name or a project

Capital letter — large letters (ABCDE) that start names and sentences

Capitalize — make the first letter or all the letters in a word into capital letters

Consistent — keeping things the same or doing them the same way each time

Noun — word that names a thing, such as an object, person, or idea

Adjective — adjective that comes from a proper noun

Proper noun — noun that names people, places, events, businesses, holidays, and titles

Disclaimer This GED Language Arts course is primarily based on the English language. It focuses on English-language reading, writing, grammar, and comprehension skills.

If you plan to take the GED exam in Spanish , you can still benefit from this course, but we strongly recommend using additional Spanish grammar and writing resources to support your preparation.

Some of the resources you can use are:

• Diccionario panhispánico de dudas

• Spanish Dict

• Punctuation

• Convevyt

• Khan Academy (esp)

• GED Maestro (Youtube Channel)

Capital Letters Bb

To capitalize a word means to make the first letter or all the letters in a word into capital letters. Capital letters (ABCDE) are the large versions for every letter in the alphabet. They are the letters that appear when you use the shift key on a keyboard – you shift up to a different case. For this reason, capital letters are sometimes called “ uppercase ” letters. Small letters (abcde) are sometimes called “ lowercase ” letters.

Proper Nouns Nouns are the words that name things. Nouns may name things you can touch or see – places, objects, and people. Or they may be the names of ideas and other non-physical things, such as love, safety, or the economy. Most nouns, like chair, kindness, or dog, are common nouns.

Some nouns, however, are known as proper nouns . When you write proper nouns, you start with a capital letter. Proper nouns include names of people, places, events, businesses, and holidays. Many adjectives that come from proper nouns are capitalized, too. For example, we use capital letters for the words Italian or Shakespearean. These are called proper adjectives .

In English, we also capitalize the word I that we use to refer to ourselves . But we do not use a capital for you or she or we . For example: On Tuesday, Bella drove me in her car when she and I went to our writing class . In the sentence, I is capitalized, but s he is not. The word me is not capitalized either.

Here are examples of proper nouns that should be capitalized:

People’s names

Bill Clinton, Nelson Mandela, Elisa, Mahmoud, Chavez

Titles that come before names

Mr. McDonald, Dr. Downs, President Obama, Ms. Markel

Place names

Africa, Montana, the White House, Cuba, the Atlantic Ocean, Liberty Avenue

Days of the week and months of the year

Wednesday, November

Other proper nouns

Labor Day, Hindu, Bank of America, Statue of Liberty

Think of your own examples for each of the above categories. Then you will remember which nouns are proper nouns.

Proper Nouns are Capitalized Proper nouns are capitalized to show that they are names, not just ordinary objects. Capitalizing these words helps readers understand what they are.

For example, you don’t need to capitalize the phrase a group of western mountains, but you would capitalize the Rocky Mountains . That lets your reader know it is the name of the mountain range. Otherwise, the reader might think you are describing what the mountains are made of – that you mean the mountains are rocky .

The summits of the Teton Range in Wyoming . Courtesy: Wikipedia

Other Uses Capital letters are used for other purposes, too. Again, it is usually to make things easier for the reader. It is how we display important information.

Here is a list of things you should capitalize, no matter what the word is:

The first word in every sentence

Use a capital letter at the beginning of every sentence.

• The tree is large.

• How do you like your eggs?

• Wow, that’s amazing!

The first word in quoted material

Use a capital letter at the beginning of quoted speech.

• When I told my mother I was having a difficult time reading signs, she said, “You may need to get some glasses.”

Headings or titles in written works

There are different ways to capitalize titles of essays and other written works.

• With essays and headings, some people just capitalize the first word – for example, My favorite place in Texas. This is called “sentence case” because the capital letters are the same as they would be in a sentence.

• Other titles capitalize every word except a, an, the, at, by, for, in, of, on, to, up, and, as, but, or, nor – for example, My Favorite Place in Texas.

Look at this part of a newspaper page. Notice that at least the first letter in every title is capitalized.

Nouns used in place of a name

If you use a common noun as a name, then it should be capitalized.

• I knew Mother was too busy working to cook dinner, so my brother and I made dinner for the family.

• “We’ve got Father and Mother, and each other,” said Beth contentedly from her corner. (From Little Women by Louisa May Alcott)

Acronyms

When an acronym (set of letters) is used instead of a formal or official title, every letter should be capitalized.

• UNHCR, if used for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees

• USA or U.S.A. if used for the United States of America

Source: FunEnglishCourse.Com

Correcting Capitalization Practice correcting capitalization in a passage of text. Read the following quotation from a blog post by a former refugee:

regarding his life before coming to united states of america, he said, “it was very bad; i was not sure about my future. there was war in iraq when i was born. there were still wars and ethnic conflicts when i left it in 2015. wars never ended until today. wars destroyed our family life. wars destroyed everything there.”

QUESTION : Which words in the above paragraph should be capitalized? Try it yourself, and then you can check the answer below for comparison.

Answer + ANSWER : You should capitalize the first word of every sentence. Capitalize the word I. Capitalize all the proper nouns. The corrected paragraph looks like this: Regarding his life before coming to A merica, he said, “It was very bad; I was not sure about my future. There was war in I raq when I was born. There were still wars and ethnic conflicts when I left it in 2015. Wars never ended until today. W ars destroyed our family life. W ars destroyed everything there.”

Be Consistent There are times when you can choose whether or not to capitalize. Some people write 6.30 a.m., while others write 6:30 AM. Some people might write “the director of operations,” while others may write, “the Director of Operations.” They are both acceptable, and the best rule is to keep it consistent . Consistent means to do something the same way, every time. If you write 6:30 AM in one place, then be consistent and use capitals, writing AM or PM, the next time you need to state the time.

GED Exam Tip Exam tip Your Language Arts test will check to make sure you do not confuse words that are alike or that people often use incorrectly. Native-born Americans and newcomer Americans often make mistakes with

these words. The GED® study guide gives the examples of to, too and two, new and knew, and your and you’re. But there are many more! 1) Here are some words that sound or look alike, and so people often use the wrong word. Make sure you know the difference in case they come up in your test: accept and except advise and advice affect and effect breath and breathe capital and capitol compliment and complement council and counsel desert and dessert lose and loose past and passed principal and principle their and there quite and quiet 2) Here is a list of words that people misuse either because they do not know the meaning or because they think the two words mean the same thing: borrow and lend compose and comprise disinterested and uninterested farther and further imply and infer lay and lie moot and mute 3) Another common writing mistake is using “ of ” when you mean “ have .” For example: Samuel would of been on time if he could of got a ride from his sister, who should of taken him but was too busy. The mistake comes because, when spoken, the “have” in would have and could have and should have sounds like “of.” But when you write it, be sure to use have: Samuel would have been on time if he could have got a ride from his sister, who should have taken him but was too busy.

Vocabulary review Acronym — set of letters (usually the first letter in a string of words) used as a name of something, such as a company name or a project

Capital Letter — large letters (ABCDE) that start names and sentences

Capitalize — make the first letter or all the letters in a word into capital letters

Consistent — keeping things the same or doing them the same way each time

Noun — word that names a thing, such as an object, person, or idea

Adjective — adjective that comes from a proper noun

Proper Noun — noun that names people, places, events, businesses, holidays, and titles

Proper nouns and proper adjectives are capitalized. Capital letters are also used for headings, titles, to start quotations, and to show the beginning of a sentence. courses.content:
In this lesson… You will learn Where do you use commas? How do you use quotation marks? What are colons and semicolons used for? When should you use question marks and exclamation points?

Words to know Clause — part of a sentence that may have a noun and verb but cannot stand completely alone

Colon — punctuation mark that introduces the next part of a sentence or group of words

Comma — punctuation mark that separates parts of a sentence

Contraction — word that has been made from two words joined and made shorter by taking out letters

Exclamation point — punctuation mark used to convey emotions or make statements stronger

Pronoun — word that takes the place of a noun, such as he, it, or they

Quotation marks — punctuation marks that shows when someone is speaking or when a writer is using someone else’s words

Semicolon — punctuation mark that connects two closely related sentences

Disclaimer This GED Language Arts course is primarily based on the English language. It focuses on English-language reading, writing, grammar, and comprehension skills.

If you plan to take the GED exam in Spanish , you can still benefit from this course, but we strongly recommend using additional Spanish grammar and writing resources to support your preparation.

Some of the resources you can use are:

• Diccionario panhispánico de dudas

• Spanish Dict

• Punctuation

• Convevyt

• Khan Academy (esp)

• GED Maestro (Youtube Channel)

Video: Basic Punctuation To begin, watch this video on punctuation.

Commas The comma is the most used punctuation mark in the English language. Commas separate lists of items and different parts of a sentence. They often help to show the writer’s meaning where it might be unclear. A comma can also change the flow between parts of your sentence.

Here are some important places to use commas:

• To separate items in a list: Raul bought scissors, tape, string, and wrapping paper.

• After introductory phrases in a sentence: Even though it was cold, they decided to go to the park.

• Before conjunctions when you join two parts of a sentence that could be complete sentences: It was warm and sunny, and so we went to the park.

• Before and after clauses that interrupt the sentence and are not necessary to the sentence: My mother, who is a doctor, is coming to dinner.

• Before quoting speech: The captain said, “Turn the boat around.”

• In addresses, especially if they are all on one line: 37 Park Drive, New York, NY 12345

• To create a pause or a break: She exclaimed, “Marwah, these flowers are beautiful!”

Quotation Marks Quotation marks show the reader that someone is speaking. They are also used to show when a writer is using someone else’s words. In both cases, the writer is quoting someone, which is why this type of punctuation is called a quotation mark .

Examples of how to use quotation marks:

“To be or not to be, that is the question.” – William Shakespeare

Jimmy said, “I like your shirt.”

I remembered that Sigmund Freud once said, “Time spent with cats is never wasted.”

Semicolons

Semicolons are used incorrectly much of the time because even many native English speakers do not understand them.

Semicolons are used to connect two sentences that are closely related. Sometimes, people use a comma when they should use a semicolon. Here is a simple rule to follow with semicolons:

If you are connecting two sentences with a conjunction, then use a comma.

If you combine two sentences without a conjunction, then use a semicolon.

For your test, you do not have to use semicolons. You won’t lose marks for not using them, but you may lose marks for using them in the wrong place. When in doubt, it’s better to keep the sentences separate or to use a conjunction. You may see them in questions that ask you to correct text. But there will not be many questions about semicolons.

Examples of sentences that correctly use semicolons:

I have to work tonight; I like working nights at my job.

I’m excited about the wedding tomorrow; I hope there will be lots of dancing and celebration.

You can see that it would be possible to write those sentences without using a semicolon. The first would work with the conjunction but . The second would be fine as two sentences.

One common mistake writers make is to use semicolons when they should be using colons.

Colons Colons are used to introduce the next part of a sentence, an idea, a group of words, or a list. An example of how to use a colon is the way we often use them in these lessons to introduce lists:

Things that make me happy are:

• birthdays

• cute babies

• chocolate

• puppies

You can use colons to introduce things in a sentence, too. For example:

It was clear what she needed to do: she must go to her brother and tell him what really happened.

But when in doubt, do not use colons in the middle of a sentence. Stick with commas, periods, and conjunctions.

Question Marks A question mark is used at the end of the sentence. The question mark tells the reader that a question is being asked.

Example: “Where are you going?”

Exclamation Points Exclamation points are also called exclamation marks. The word exclaim means to say something in an outburst of emotion. An exclamation point can be used to communicate emotions or to make statements stronger. It adds an element of excitement. It can be used to break up a long, serious essay.

Examples of where to use exclamation points:

No! I do not like green eggs and ham!

He was so courageous!

Challenge accepted!

Exclamation points should not be used very often ! People use the exclamation point more than they need to! If you use too many, your reader may begin to question what you say! Be cautious when using the exclamation point!

Look again at the paragraph above. Can you see why the exclamation mark is not used very often?

People use (and overuse) exclamations in text messages, on social media, and when writing emails. Exclamation points are used more often in books for younger children than for older children, to add excitement. Using a lot of exclamation points is unprofessional. Avoid doing so when you are writing an essay, a job application, or anything for your work.

GED Exam Tip Exam tip Apostrophes ( ’ ) are a challenge for English learners and everyone else trying to write correct English. But you can use apostrophes correctly in your language arts test. Apostrophes are used to show possession. Possession is when something owns or belongs to something else. To show possession, you add an apostrophe followed by an s : the chair’s legs , or Ada’s computer . Apostrophes get a bit confusing when you want to show possession with words that already end in s . You can follow these rules: If the noun is singular and ends in s, add ’ s: The class’s attitude was positive If the noun is plural and ends in s, add only an apostrophe: The flowers’ color was a bright yellow To show possession on a name ending in s , some writers add just ’ , others add ’s, and others use both forms depending on the sound of the word. However, Tomas’s car and Tomas’ car would both be considered correct in your language arts test. You don’t need apostrophes to show possession with pronouns . Pronouns already have their own words to show possession. Here are common pronouns and their possessive forms: I/me = my or mine you = your or yours he/him = his she/her = her or hers we/us = our or ours they/them = their or theirs it = its who = whose You do not need an apostrophe with any of those words. Apostrophes are used to show missing letters. Contractions are words that have been joined and made shorter by taking out letters. The apostrophes go in the place of the missing letters. For example: “Who’s going to the store?” is short for “Who is going to the store?” “You’ve done well” is short for “You have done well.” “It’s raining” is short for “It is raining.” Apostrophes are NOT used to show plurals Here are two VERY common mistakes that people make: You do not need an apostrophe in plurals or other words ending in s unless you want to show possession. So if Mr and Mrs Abadi invite you to their house, it is the (plural) Abadis who invite you, not the Abadi’s. But the plural Abadis may be having a party at their house, in which case you are attending the Abadis’ party! In the same way, you may have been born in the 1970s and have a collection of CDs. But you don’t need apostrophes to write that. Avoid common apostrophe mistakes Now that you know the rules, you will see incorrect apostrophes everywhere: on signs, in advertisements, and on websites! But you can avoid the most common errors: Don’t mix up (possessive) its and (contraction) it’s Don’t mix up (contraction) you’re and (possessive) your Don’t mix up (contraction) they’re or (possessive) their with there Just because a verb or noun ends in s , do not make the mistake of inserting an apostrophe before the s .

Video: Using Apostrophes Watch this video to review when to use apostrophes.

Vocabulary review

Clause — part of a sentence that may have a noun and verb but cannot stand completely alone

Colon — punctuation mark that introduces the next part of a sentence or group of words

Comma — punctuation mark that separates parts of a sentence

Contraction — word that has been made from two words joined and made shorter by taking out letters

Exclamation Point — punctuation mark used to convey emotions or make statements stronger

Pronoun — word that takes the place of a noun, such as he, it, or they

Quotation Marks — punctuation marks that shows when someone is speaking or when a writer is using someone else’s words

Semicolon — punctuation mark that connects two closely related sentences

Summary What we learned Commas can be used to make things clear, to separate parts of a sentence, and in lists. Quotation marks show the reader that the writer is quoting someone. Semicolons connect two sentences that are closely related. Colons introduce the next part of a sentence, an idea, a group of words, or a list. Question marks indicate that a question is being asked. Exclamation points show emotions or make statements stronger.

courses.content:
In this lesson… You will learn Why should I take the time to plan my essay? What is a thesis? What are supporting ideas? How do you present the other side? How do you make an essay map?

Words to know Argument — statement or series of statements for or against something using evidence and examples. For example, you may argue that vegetables are the best food because they are good for you

Counter — oppose or challenge

Opposing — different; in contrast to one another

Outline — structure of an essay without the details

Thesis — viewpoint your essay is taking

Plan Your Essay Why should I take the time to plan my essay?

You will have 45 minutes to complete your essay. If you spend a few minutes thinking about how to present your ideas, the writing will go more easily and quickly. This is true no matter what you are writing about. A good plan will help your writing stay focused on the topic. You will feel more comfortable writing and that will help you stay calm in your test.

Pre-writing

Planning is sometimes called “pre-writing.” Pre-writing helps you put your thoughts and ideas on paper. You can figure out what is important to include in the essay and what is not. Pre-writing also helps the writer decide the order of the paragraphs.

Planning and organizing your essay before writing is worth the time that it takes. But you should not spend so long pre-writing that you don’t have time to write! Here is a suggested time frame:

• Thinking about what you want to say and making notes: 10 minutes

• Organizing your ideas and sentences: 5 minutes

• Writing your essay: 25 minutes

• Reading and correcting your essay: 5 minutes

Define Your Thesis In the GED essay section, you will be given a passage (or sometimes two passages) on a certain topic. The passages might present different points of view, or they might just give different information about the same topic.

Your job is to write an essay about the topic. The testers want to see if you can organize your thoughts, make an argument, give examples, and write clearly. No matter what, the process is the same: you need to choose a main idea (called a thesis) and develop your ideas to support it.

What is a thesis? A thesis is the main point of your essay—it’s the position or opinion you are taking about the topic. You should include your thesis in the first paragraph, in a simple, clear sentence. This sentence tells the reader what your essay will be about. It’s okay to include a little bit about why you believe this, but you should leave the details for the rest of your essay.

How do I choose a thesis? There is no "wrong" thesis, as long as it is logical and based on the passage you are given. For example, let’s say you are given two different opinions about what makes a good parent. One opinion might say a good parent gives a lot of attention and guidance. The other opinion might say a good parent provides opportunities and financial security.

Depending on what the passage says, your thesis could be one of these:

• If you agree with the first view : A good parent spends time with their children and teaches them important life lessons.

• If you agree with the second view : A good parent makes sure their children have the resources and opportunities they need to succeed.

It doesn’t matter if you personally agree or disagree with these statements. The key is to use information from the passage to support your thesis. Both theses work because they are based on the topic given. However, it would be wrong to write about something off-topic, like your favorite food!

Include Supporting Ideas When writing your essay, it's important to include examples that support your main idea, or thesis statement. To do this, choose a thesis statement that you can back up with several strong points.

For example, let's say you've been given two texts with different opinions on public transportation.

The essay question is: Should public transportation be free?

You could choose either side:

• Public transportation should be free because it helps people get to work and school more easily, and it's better for the environment than everyone driving their own cars.

• Public transportation should be paid for by those who use it because it costs money to run, and not everyone uses public transportation.

If you're asked to write about the arguments in a text, you'll need to use examples from the text to support your points. You can pick the side you agree with, but it may be easier to write your essay if you choose the argument that has the strongest supporting evidence.

Include Counter-Arguments In an essay expressing your opinion, especially when you are comparing two viewpoints, you should include both sides of the issue to make the strongest argument. Writing about the other side of an argument, the side you don’t agree with, makes you seem knowledgeable, so the reader is more likely to believe you have really thought about what you are writing. The “other side” of the argument is called the counter-argument . It counters , or opposes, the original argument.

As an example, suppose that you are writing about two passages of text that discusses the idea that American culture is better than other cultures. You need to agree or disagree in your essay.

Example of an argument : "American culture is better than other cultures because it promotes individual freedom and offers many opportunities for personal success. People from all over the world move to the United States to seek a better life, which shows that American values are attractive globally."

Example of a counter-argument : "However, some may argue that other cultures, such as those in Asian or European countries, offer stronger family and community values. These cultures prioritize collective well-being over individual success, which can lead to a more supportive social environment."

When writing your essay, after presenting the counter-argument, you would then explain why you believe your original argument is still stronger.

For example: "While other cultures may emphasize community values, American culture’s focus on individual freedom allows people to pursue their own goals and shape their own futures, which is a key reason why many choose to immigrate to the U.S."

Video: Writing a well-planned essay Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

Video Transcript + When studying for your GED Language Arts test, it is helpful to know how to prepare an essay. This starts with having a great outline. As you read the text you will be writing about, make notes of your thesis and the supporting ideas; including counter-arguments. Next, you will need to organize your ideas and sentences into a plan, or essay map. An essay map or outline will show: Your thesis statement The thesis will go in your first paragraph with one or two introductory sentences. Two or three supporting ideas These can be arguments, examples, details, and counter-arguments. Make sure they are relevant to

and/or supportive of your thesis. Organize your ideas into an order that makes sense. The essay map below shows three “main idea” blocks. Each of those should be a paragraph that covers a separate supporting idea. Each paragraph will contain up to three supporting details, and you can note those as well. Your conclusion You will write a concluding statement that sums up your ideas and reminds the reader of your thesis. Your essay map doesn’t have to be perfect, and you don’t need to spend a lot of time on it. Even spending ten minutes will help you write your essay. Once you have an essay map on paper, it will guide you through writing the essay. In the next lesson, we’ll show you how to do that! This diagram shows an essay map. The topic, including your thesis statement, will become your first paragraph. The three main ideas will be the middle paragraphs of your essay. They will support your thesis. The conclusion will form the last paragraph.

Vocabulary review Argument — statement or series of statements for or against something using evidence and examples. For example, you may argue that vegetables are the best food because they are good for you.

Counter — oppose or challenge

Opposing — different; in contrast to one another

Outline — structure of an essay without the details

Thesis — viewpoint your essay is taking

Summary What we learned Organizing and planning your essay will help the writing go more easily and quickly. Your 45 minutes of essay-writing might include about 15 minutes pre-writing or mapping your essay, 25 minutes writing, and 5 minutes to check and correct your essay. A one-sentence thesis statement explains the position you will take on the subject. Supporting ideas give evidence for your thesis and show why you have taken your position. Presenting a counter-argument shows you have thought about both sides and gives you a chance to show that your own argument is more logical or has more supporting evidence. A good essay map shows the thesis and supporting ideas and helps you put them in order.

“Over the next few years, my main goal is to obtain a college degree from St. John’s University in Collegeville. This goal will be very difficult to obtain and I will need to work hard at it. Three things that will affect the outcome of my goal are: how much money I can raise to pay for it, how much time I am willing to spend studying, and my dedication to training for football.

This is a huge sum of money. It is not made easier by the fact that my parents will be able to contribute very little towards my education. Thus I am forced to rely on scholarships, grants, and loans from the government and other agencies. I have already taken some action by applying for scholarships, but I will have to apply again next year. I received a $7,500 scholarship from St. John’s and they have also given me some grants. The rest of the money will have to come from student loans and a job.
The next area that will affect my goal is the classroom. This is important because the main point of college is to prepare oneself for a successful career. In college, I will need to apply myself and take time to study every night. Sometimes I may be forced to give up things that I would rather do, but I must if I am going to achieve my goal. I must create a relationship with my professors because they will help.

I must spend many hours in the weight room gaining strength and quickness. I believe all of the hard work will pay off.
If I can do these three things, I will successfully complete my goal of graduating from college. If this goal is achieved, I believe I will be well on my way to a successful life.”

courses.content:
In this lesson… You will learn What are the three parts of an essay? How do you write a good introduction? How do you write a good body paragraph? How do you write a good conclusion?

Words to know Introduction — first paragraph in an essay that states the topic and thesis statement

Body Paragraphs — paragraphs between the introduction and conclusion that details and supporting examples related to the topic

Conclusion — last part of something, especially a last part that includes a summary of what came before

Summarize — briefly cover the important points

Main Parts of an Essay The three main parts of an essay are the introduction (the beginning), the body (the middle), and the conclusion (the ending).

The introduction includes your thesis statement. The body contains the supporting arguments. The conclusion summarizes the thesis and supporting arguments to make your point clear.

Following are some tips on writing the different parts of an essay:

Beginning:

• State the main idea or position. It begins with a topic sentence/thesis statement. The beginning restates the question and sets the stage to answer the prompt.

Middle:

• Answer the question first.

• Provide important information the author stated and meant. This is where you go to the text(s) and provide examples/evidence and important details to support the answer.

• Include sample phrases to introduce each text reference include: …stated; in the text…; for example…

• Include background information as required through the prompt.

Ending:

• Write a closing that summarizes the position taken or restates the thesis statement in a different way.

A Good Introduction The first paragraph of an essay is one of the most important parts. It introduces the topic and tells the reader what the essay will be about.

To grab the reader's attention, you need to clearly mention the main points the essay will cover. For example, if you’re writing an essay about the benefits of exercise, your first paragraph might mention that you will discuss physical health, mental well-being, and how exercise can improve sleep. The introduction also includes a thesis statement—a sentence that expresses your main point or opinion.

A thesis statement for this topic could be, "Regular exercise improves both mental and physical health, making it a key factor for a better quality of life." By reading the first paragraph, your audience will know the essay’s main ideas and the order in which you will discuss them.

When writing an introduction, you can follow this sequence:

• The first sentence introduces the topic (e.g., "Exercise is essential for maintaining a healthy lifestyle").

• The next 1–3 sentences outline the ideas you will discuss in the body of your essay (e.g., "It benefits physical health, mental well-being, and improves sleep").

• The last sentence is your thesis statement, which clearly states your point of view (e.g., "Exercise should be a regular part of everyone’s routine because it leads to significant improvements in both mental and physical health").

Body of an Essay The body of an essay is the part between the introduction and the conclusion. These are called the supporting paragraphs . They explain and give reasons to support your main point, or thesis, showing why you believe your thesis is correct.

In most essays, there are two or three supporting body paragraphs. If you have fewer than that, it might look like you didn’t fully develop your ideas. However, because you often have limited time to plan and write and essay in GED test, it's usually best to write no more than three body paragraphs.

Here’s an example: If your thesis is “Exercise is important for mental health,” your body paragraphs should each give a different reason why exercise helps mental health. One paragraph could explain how exercise reduces stress, another could talk about how it improves sleep, and a third might focus on how it boosts your mood.

A good essay usually presents its strongest or most important reason first. The second-best reason comes next, and so on. For instance, in our example, if you think reducing stress is the strongest benefit of exercise, you’d put that reason in the first body paragraph.

Sometimes, though, you may want to change the order of your paragraphs. For example, you might start with an argument that goes against your thesis, so you can prove it wrong. The key is to have one clear idea in each paragraph and make sure each paragraph supports your main point.

So, if you're writing about exercise and mental health, your first paragraph might explain how some people believe exercise doesn’t help, but then your next paragraphs can show why exercise is actually good for mental health, challenging that argument.

Quick Tips for Writing Body of an Essay

• The body consists of supporting paragraphs that explain and give reasons for your thesis.

• Include 2-3 body paragraphs for a well-developed essay.

• Each paragraph should focus on a separate reason that supports your thesis.

• A common structure: strongest reason first, second-best reason second, and so on.

• It’s okay to present counterarguments first, then challenge them with your reasons.

• Each paragraph should clearly explain one idea and connect to the thesis.

• Keep it clear and simple—especially important when writing under time constraints like in the GED test.

Writing a Good Body In a good essay, each body paragraph focuses on one supporting idea. You have already chosen the supporting ideas in your essay map.

Start each paragraph with one sentence to introduce the main idea of the paragraph. Then give details to support the idea. If possible, there should be more than one example or detail to support each argument. Each of your supporting paragraphs should have at least four sentences.

For example, in an essay about important aspects of work, a writer mentions pay in her introduction. She says, “Pay is an important consideration for me.” Therefore, one of the body paragraphs will be about pay. She could say:

“How much money a job pays is very important. I have seen what happens when people do not make enough money. They can have a hard time paying bills, and their lives often become difficult. I know that I need to make enough money to pay my bills. That is why pay is so important to me.”

The writer began the paragraph by introducing the topic, or main idea, of the paragraph. Then, the writer added details to support the main point. Those details included an example. There is also some personal observation . That led the writer to state again why it is important to earn enough money.

Writing a Good Conclusion The conclusion is the last paragraph of the essay. It is important, but it doesn’t have to be very long. You have already stated your thesis and provided several convincing reasons to support your thesis statement. The conclusion will summarize the essay and restate the thesis statement.

A good concluding paragraph does three things well:

• Refers back to the essay’s main topic

• Summarizes the ideas in the body by mentioning all the topics

• Reminds the reader that the essay proved the thesis

Video: Answering the Question Video Transcript + Some people find that all it takes to write an essay to open your computer and start typing. However, in order to write an essay, much more planning is required. It is a good idea to follow a

number of important phases in the process of writing an essay. Especially, if this is your first time writing an essay, you struggle with writing and want to improve your skills, and you are being asked to write an essay in a short amount of time. It may seem obvious, but we are going to say it anyway: when you write your essay, answer the question ! You may write a beautiful essay, but if it does not directly and fully address the question, you will not score well. Here are some things you can ask yourself to make sure you have answered the question: What is the question asking? Is it asking whether I agree or disagree? Is it asking which of two views is better presented or better supported? Make sure you know what the question is and keep it in mind as you write. For example, the question could be, what do you think about public health and individual freedom? Am I following the directions? Look carefully at the words in the question. For example, if the directions say “ discuss ” the issues in the text, that is your sign that you need to comment on them, not just say what they are. If it says “ present both sides ,” you know you must do more than just take one position and argue for it. If it says, “ explain which argument is better supported, ” then don’t forget to explain why one or the other is better. Have I written enough? GED guidelines say that fully answering the essay question “often requires 4 to 7 paragraphs of 3 to 7 sentences each … A response that is significantly shorter could put you in danger of scoring a 0 just for not showing enough of your writing skills.” Give yourself a minimum of four paragraphs, a maximum of five paragraphs, with at least three sentences in each paragraph. Have I done all the things asked? If the directions list three things to do, you should do all of them. For example, you may be asked to include an example from your own experience, so do that. It may also say, provide evidence from the text, so you should do that too . Finally, if the directions ask why you have taken a certain position, make sure you give good reasons.

Video: Parts of an Essay Watch this video to review the parts of an essay and how to write them:

Example of a Good Essay Read the example essay below. It is about the topic of vaccinations. Imagine that it was written in response to text that examined reasons for vaccinating children against disease and reasons opposing those vaccinations. Imagine that the prompt asked the student to write in favor of one of the two arguments and give reasons for supporting it.

• Look at how the introduction introduces the topic and mentions its main opposing points (vaccines are important to public health, but some people disagree with them). The writer then presents a thesis, and in the same sentence summarizes the arguments he or she will present in the essay.

• Notice that each of the three body paragraphs relate to a separate but relevant aspect of the topic. Notice also that paragraph 3 introduces a counter-argument and shows why it is weak compared to the arguments the writer supports.

• The names in parentheses show the sources of information that were included in the original text. The writer used the text as supporting evidence.

• When you read the conclusion, you will see that it summarizes the points made before and strongly restates the thesis based on the arguments presented in the essay.

Paragraph 1: Introduction with thesis statement (underlined) and three supporting arguments.

Since Edward Jenner introduced the first successful smallpox vaccine by injecting an eight-year-old boy with cowpox pus in 1796, vaccines have been an important part of public health care around the world (Edward Jenner). Yet today, many parents choose not to vaccinate their children. Because vaccines are widely supported by research, have few side effects, and have proven successful in halting the spread of disease, I believe it is important that all parents continue to vaccinate their children.

Paragraph 2: Topic sentence and examples that develop the first reason by giving examples.

Major health organizations, including the Centers for Disease Control and the World Health Organization, recommend vaccination. The value of vaccination is supported by research from around the world, and researchers are constantly working to improve the safety and effectiveness of vaccines. Epidemiologists, the scientists whose jobs study the outbreak of disease, all recommend vaccination.

Paragraph 3: T opic sentence develops the second reason, giving facts and statistics to support the statement.

Many parents worry about the safety of vaccines. While side effects do occur, they are usually minor, like redness or swelling around the site of an injection. In Canada, only about one in a million doses of vaccine leads to serious side effects (“Fact and Fiction”). The most famous study linking vaccines to autism, one which got many parents worried about vaccination, has been proven false and the doctor who conducted the study has had his medical license taken away (Triggle).

Paragraph 4: topic sentence develops third reason, giving an example.

Around the world, increased vaccination leads to better public health. Diseases like smallpox and polio which once killed and disabled millions of people are virtually unknown today thanks to immunization programs. Yet in countries like Afghanistan and Pakistan where the Taliban discourage immunization, rates of polio are on the rise again (Nordland).

Paragraph 5: Conclusion and restatement of thesis followed by summary of reasons.

And when you have children, please get them vaccinated. The risks are minimal and you’ll not only be following the best advice of medical science and protecting your own child from disease; you’ll be helping in the fight to eradicate infectious diseases in your community and around the world.

Vocabulary review Introduction — The first paragraph in an essay. It states the topic and thesis statement.

Body Paragraphs — The body paragraphs follow the introduction. The body paragraphs are written in between the introduction and conclusion. They contain details and supporting examples related to the topic.

Conclusion — The conclusion is the last paragraph of the essay. It summarizes what came before. The conclusion briefly covers the important points.

Summary What we learned The three main parts of an essay are the introduction, the body and the conclusion. The introductory paragraph states the topic, says what is coming, and includes your thesis statement. The body of the essay contains two or three main ideas that support the thesis. Body paragraphs should each state their own main idea followed by some details or examples that explain that idea. The concluding paragraph refers back to the essay’s main topic, summarizes the ideas in the body, and reminds the reader of its thesis.

courses.content:
In this lesson… You will learn What is a transition? Why and how are transitions used? Where is the best place to put transitions? What are the different kinds of transition words?

Words to know Conclusion — ending that draws parts together and presents the final idea

Connect — join together

Emphasize — make more important

Exception — something that is excluded from or does not follow a general rule

Prove — demonstrate the truth with evidence or a strong argument

Sequence — order or pattern

Transition — change from one thing to the next

Using Transitions A transition is a change.

In writing, transitions are used when you change from one idea to another idea.

Transitions connect ideas and introduce new ideas. You can use transitions within paragraphs to connect thoughts together. You can also use them when you move from one paragraph to the next. Transitions help the reader understand how the thoughts in the two separate paragraphs are connected to each other. They also help the flow of your writing.

A transition may be in the last sentence of a paragraph, the first sentence of the next paragraph, or in both places. Usually, the best place for a transition between paragraphs is in the first sentence of the second of two paragraphs.

Video: Transition Words Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

Transition Words that Add The following examples include words and phrases that will help you transition from one sentence, phrase, or paragraph to the next. By adding a transition, we can see how the different ideas fit together.

Transition words that add

and also again and then besides equally important finally further furthermore nor too next lastly what's more moreover in addition additionally first second third

Without Transition Words Transition words are crucial for connecting ideas and improving the flow of writing. Without them, sentences can feel choppy or disconnected.

Here are a few examples to illustrate the differences in the sentences with and without transition words:

With Transition Words:

• Example : "I wanted to go to the park. However, it started raining." Effect : The word "however" indicates a contrast between wanting to go to the park and the reality of rain.

• Example : "I studied hard for the test. As a result, I passed with flying colors." Effect : "As a result" shows the cause-and-effect relationship between studying and passing the test.

Without Transition Words:

• Example : "I wanted to go to the park. It started raining." Effect : The sentences feel separate and lack clarity about the relationship between the two ideas.

• Example : "I studied hard for the test. I passed with flying colors." Effect : Without "as a result," the connection between studying and passing is unclear.

Summary

Using transition words helps clarify relationships between ideas, making writing more cohesive and easier to understand. Incorporating these words can significantly improve their writing skills.

Transition Words that Compare whereas nevertheless up against meanwhile but on the contrary balanced against after all yet by comparison but in contrast on the other hand where although although this may be true however compared to conversely

Transition Words that Prove I like schools in the United States because public school education is free. I don’t like schools in the United States because all of the classes are taught in English.

Here are the sentences with transition words in place:

I like schools in the United States because public school education is free. However , I don’t like that all of the classes are taught in English.

Transition words that prove

because evidently in fact for furthermore in addition since moreover in any case for this reason besides that is obviously indeed

Here are examples of sentences that need transition words:

I know more than my sister. I’m twelve years older than her. She hasn’t started school yet.

Here are the sentences with transition words in place:

I’m twelve years older than my sister and she hasn’t started school yet. For this reason, I know more than she does.

Transition Words that Show Exception yet despite still of course however once in a while nevertheless sometimes in spite of

Here are some examples of sentences that need transition words:

I like to walk in the hills. It’s more windy in the hills than in town. It’s not much fun walking in the wind. I need fresh air and exercise even when it’s windy.

Here are the same sentences with transition words in place:I like to walk in the hills, yet it’s more windy in the hills than in town. Of course, it’s not much fun walking in the wind. Nevertheless, I need fresh air and exercise even when it’s windy.

Transition Words that Show Time immediately then second thereafter later next soon previously and then after a few hours formerly before that finally first

We will add on to the example from above:

I like to walk in the hills, yet it’s more windy in the hills than in town. Of course, it’s not much fun walking in the wind. Nevertheless, I need fresh air and exercise even when it’s windy. When I get cold, I like to drink a hot cup of tea to get warm again.

Here are the same sentences with a transition sentence added:

I like to walk in the hills, yet it’s more windy in the hills than in town. Of course, it’s not much fun walking in the wind. Nevertheless, I need fresh air and exercise even when it’s windy. After walking in the wind, I’m often quite cold . When I get cold, I like to drink a hot cup of tea to get warm again.

Including the transition helps the reader connect the ideas.

Repeating with Transition Words in brief in other words as I have said in summary as I have noted that is as has been noted to summarize

The following paragraph has some transition words. It could use another transition when it adds a step:

You can connect all kinds of ideas if you use transitional words. As an illustration, let’s look at the sentences: “I know more than my sister. I’m twelve years older than her.” Let’s look at how a transition could improve those sentences. The two ideas would make much more sense if they were connected. We’ll put them together to read: “I know more than my sister because I’m twelve years older than her.”

If you add transition words that show the sequence, the reader can follow the main ideas better:You can connect all kinds of ideas if you use transitional words. As an illustration, let’s look at the sentences: “I know more than my sister. I’m twelve years older than her.” Next, let’s look at how a transition could improve those sentences. The two ideas would make much more sense if they were connected. Therefore , we’ll put them together to read: “I know more than my sister because I’m twelve years older than her.”

Next, let’s look at how a transition could improve those sentences. The two ideas would make much more sense if they were connected. Therefore, we’ll put them together to read: “I know more than my sister because I’m twelve years older than her.” We use transitions to make sense of what we write, to connect parts, and to make our essays easier and more enjoyable to read.”

Next, let’s look at how a transition could improve those sentences. The two ideas would make much more sense if they were connected. Therefore, we’ll put them together to read: “I know more than my sister because I’m twelve years older than her.” In conclusion, we use transitions to make sense of what we write, to connect parts, and to make our essays easier and more enjoyable to read.

GED Exam Tip

Exam tip You’ve learned a lot about using the English language in this class. Your testers will be looking for organization and for correct grammar. But they will also be looking to see that you write clearly and in a way that engages your reader. Here are some tips for writing clearly: Vary your sentence structure – don’t start every sentence the same way or make all sentences the same length. Write to interest your readers, not to impress them with how many long words you know. Be direct – don’t use 50 words when 5 words will do. Be relevant – avoid including unnecessary information. Use transitional words and phrases to connect sentences and improve flow, but don’t overuse them. Don’t repeat yourself except for summarizing. In your summary, find another, shorter way to say what you have already said. Very importantly, leave yourself a few minutes for proofreading after you finish writing. Quickly correct any mistakes in grammar, sentence fragments or run-ons, wrong words, and confused wording. Your last-minute corrections may save you from losing many points!

questions.prompt:
DIRECTIONS: Read the following stimulus material
“Tweens” Are Ready for Cell Phones
A speech by Deborah Pendergast at the Safer Kids Summit
Thank you for inviting me to the first “Safer Kids Summit.” We are here to discuss ways to keep our children safe in an increasingly complex world. Today’s focus is on technology — specifically on the ideal age to give kids their own cell phones. As a representative of a large telecommunications company, I receive many inquiries from parents on this topic, and this is what I tell them: It depends on the child, of course, but in general, age 10 is just about right.
A 2012 survey by the National Consumers League backs me up. The survey found that almost 60 percent of children ages 8 to 12 already have cell phones. These “tweens” can contact their parents at any time, and vice versa, giving the kids a sense of empowerment and their parents a feeling of security. Caroline Knorr, of the group Common Sense Media, says, “We want our kids to be independent, to be able to walk home from school and play at the playground without us. We want them to have that old-fashioned, fun experience of being on their own, and cell phones can help with that.” Picture the following scenario: You told your fourth-grader that you would pick her up after school, but you are stuck in traffic. She is waiting for you …and waiting, and waiting. But if you both have cell phones, you can call her to let her know you are delayed, and she can go back inside the school, where there are adults around. You both breathe a sigh of relief.
Psychologists tell us that the period between ages 10 and 12 is one of growing independence. It is a time to teach children about responsibility, and to give them opportunities to earn our trust. Providing a 10-year-old with a cell phone offers an ideal way to achieve these goals and gives parents peace of mind as well.
QUESTION: What is the main argument, or point?
questions.explanation:
Answer:
d) Cell phones can help tweens learn to be safe.
Explanation:
The speaker emphasizes how cell phones provide a sense of security for both children and their parents, as well as opportunities for tweens to learn responsibility and independence.

options.label: B
options.body: Tweens are not ready for cell phones.

options.label: C
options.body: Tweens are children in between elementary school and teenagers.

options.label: D
options.body: Cell phones can help tweens learn to be safe.

Thank you for inviting me to the first “Safer Kids Summit.” We are here to discuss ways to keep our children safe in an increasingly complex world. Today’s focus is on technology — specifically on the ideal age to give kids their own cell phones. As a representative of a large telecommunications company, I receive many inquiries from parents on this topic, and this is what I tell them: It depends on the child, of course, but in general, age 10 is just about right.
A 2012 survey by the National Consumers League backs me up. The survey found that almost 60 percent of children ages 8 to 12 already have cell phones. These “tweens” can contact their parents at any time, and vice versa, giving the kids a sense of empowerment and their parents a feeling of security. Caroline Knorr, of the group Common Sense Media, says, “We want our kids to be independent, to be able to walk home from school and play at the playground without us. We want them to have that old-fashioned, fun experience of being on their own, and cell phones can help with that.” Picture the following scenario: You told your fourth-grader that you would pick her up after school, but you are stuck in traffic. She is waiting for you …and waiting, and waiting. But if you both have cell phones, you can call her to let her know you are delayed, and she can go back inside the school, where there are adults around. You both breathe a sigh of relief.
Psychologists tell us that the period between ages 10 and 12 is one of growing independence. It is a time to teach children about responsibility, and to give them opportunities to earn our trust. Providing a 10-year-old with a cell phone offers an ideal way to achieve these goals and gives parents peace of mind as well.
QUESTION: What is one piece of evidence that supports the main point?

Answer:
b) The period between ages 10 and 12 is one of growing independence. It is a time to teach children about responsibility.

Answer
b

Source Material #2
Wait Until They Are Older
A speech by Linda Sidner  at the Safer Kids Summit
Good morning! I come to this topic as a parent and a veteran teacher of so-called “tweens.” I love kids this age for their curiosity and energy, but those same qualities can lead to trouble if not overseen by adults. That’s why giving children their own phones actually makes them less safe, not more. I believe that the best age for a cell phone is 16, the point at which we consider kids grown-up enough to learn to drive — and even then, parents must set firm limits on phone use!
Why are tweens with phones less safe? For one thing, parents may be lulled into a false sense of security if their kids have phones. They may become careless about knowing where their child is and who he is with, thinking, “I can always reach him on his phone.” For another, cell phones give children access to all the frightening, dangerous, and inappropriate sites on the internet, with no parent nearby to monitor this activity.
But perhaps the most worrisome aspect of giving cell phones to children is the rise in “cyberbullying” or “text bullying.” Text bullying means using a cell phone to send cruel, embarrassing, or false text messages to or about someone. In one study, researcher Elizabeth Englander found that by middle school, over 90% of children report that they use their cell phones to text or go onto the internet. She also found that in grades 3 through 5, between 14 and 19 percent of children reported being victims of cyberbullying. What if it’s your child on the receiving end of this cruelty? Or, perhaps worse, what if your child is the bully? Children of this age are simply not mature enough to handle this technology, and we shouldn’t expect them to be. It’s our job as adults to protect them. That’s why I say: It’s better to wait.

: Analyze the arguments presented in the two speeches. Which position has more evidence than the other? Explain how one position is better supported than the other. Incorporate relevant and specific evidence from both sources to support your argument. Remember, the better-argued position is not necessarily the position that you agree with.

Parenting Education Should Be Mandatory
By Kai Fernandez, APRN, the
Freeport Times
As a nurse practitioner in a pediatric office, I had to complete extensive training and obtain a license before I could examine my first toddler. Many jobs, from barber to pilot, involve specific training. But for the most important job — raising children to be responsible adults —no training is required, and children and society suffer the results of this lack of knowledge. The time has come to correct this situation. Before they can be discharged from the hospital, first-time parents should be required to take parenting classes.
Just as we equip new drivers with a learner’s permit and instruction, we must also equip new parents with the skills they need. While some people might believe that this is the “nanny state” stepping on the rights of individuals, I am not suggesting that there is only one “correct” style of parenting. But there is basic information about infants and children that every parent should be required to know, including nutrition, health and safety, and stages of child development. Knowing how to safely bathe a baby, for example, would prevent many tragedies. Understanding that babies are crying to communicate, not to be “naughty,” helps parents adjust their expectations and their behavior.
And parent education works. According to the Centers for Disease Control, for example, the “Safe To Sleep” campaign has reduced the number of deaths from Sudden Infant Death Syndrome by fifty percent since 1994 just by teaching parents to put babies to bed on their backs. Conversely, uninformed parenting hurts not only children, but the rest of us as well. A study by the Department of Education in England found that children whose parents use harsh or inconsistent discipline are more likely to have poor attention spans, low levels of literacy, and antisocial behavior.
In cultures where extended families are the rule, raising children is a group effort. But in the modern world, new parents are on their own. It is our obligation as a society to make sure they have the skills to do their best in this challenging job. Making parenting classes mandatory is a step towards this goal.
QUESTION: What is the main argument, or point?

b) First-time parents should be required to take parenting classes.
Explanation:
The author emphasizes that parenting education should be mandatory for first-time parents to ensure they are equipped with essential skills and knowledge, which can benefit both children and society.

courses.content:
In this lesson… You will learn How do you write about two points of view? What guidelines do you follow when writing your essay? What is the stimulus material? What is the prompt? How are essays scored?

Words to know Better-supported — has more evidence and good reasoning to support it

Credible — convincing and believable

Evaluate — make a decision or form an idea about how good something is

Prompt — something to get you started

Video: Writing Points of View Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

Video Transcript + You have learned how to plan an essay, how to write the different parts, and how to use transitions in your writing. You will need to put these new skills into practice as you compare points of view. The GED test in particular will ask you to evaluate which position is the better-supported one. “Better-supported” means the argument that has the most evidence and good reasoning to support it. The test is not asking which opinion you agree with. It’s asking you to look at both arguments, or opinions, in the text and say which is better, and why. How to write about two points of view The first step, as you have already learned, is planning your essay. You should use the essay map to organize your ideas. Here are samples of maps you can use to organize your ideas. Name: Date: Class Period: Looking at Both Sides of an Issue Directions: Begin by stating the question in the box provided. Then, in the “Yes” column, give reasons, examples, or facts that could be stated in support of the question. In the “No” column, give reasons, examples, or facts that could be stated in dispute of the question. State your opinion in the conclusion box. Yes Question No Reasons Conclusion Name: Date: Class Period: Persuasion Map Directions: Write your position and the reasons that justify it in the boxes indicated. Then, write the facts, details, and examples that support each reason in the dotted boxes. Draw, and connect more boxes if needed. Reason 1 Reason 2 Reason 3 Position Start your essay with an introduction. Introduce the topic and state your thesis in the first paragraph. Your thesis should clearly state which of the two arguments you think is better, based on evidence from the text. It does not need to explain your reasons yet. Next, you are going to give details to explain your thesis. Since you are comparing two viewpoints, your next two paragraphs could describe the two sides of the argument. Point out the weak points and strong points as you write, using evidence from the passage. Both viewpoints will probably have some weaker points and some stronger points. The second paragraph can be about the position that you do support and paragraph three can cover the position you do not support. Or, you can start with the argument you are not supporting, if that fits the material better. That way, when you are writing paragraph three about the position you do support, you can show how much more credible it is. In the fourth paragraph, you can explain your viewpoint. Persuade the reader why your thesis is correct, based on what you have just shown them about the two positions. Then, write a short conclusion paragraph. There is no rule to say an essay must have five paragraphs. If you have made your views clear in the second and third paragraphs, your explanation and conclusion might be the same paragraph. In that case, your essay will have four paragraphs instead of five. No matter the number of paragraphs, your extended response needs to: State your thesis Show both sides Give evidence from the text Make a good conclusion

Video: Extended Response Now, watch the following video to help you organize your extended response

GED Exam Tip Exam tip Whichever test you are taking and whatever kind of essay you are writing, you will almost certainly be using supporting evidence from a text or texts. If you use evidence in your essay, you will score well. Here are some tips for presenting evidence in your essay. Use quotes from the text to give evidence for your argument, or to give examples of the author’s opinions, or both. When you choose your thesis or argument, make sure there is some good evidence in the text to back it up. To introduce your evidence, you can quote directly or paraphrase (put it on your own words). You can use phrases such as: According to the text, ……………. The first text says, “…………… The writer states, “…..” For example, the article explains that …….. In her letter, Dr M claimed ………… When you use direct quotes, make sure you copy them correctly and use quotation marks. If you are putting the evidence into your own words, do not use quotation marks. Show you know the difference between good evidence and opinions. To do this, you can contrast two quotes from the text – one that shows good logic or facts, and one that is an opinion or appears to be rhetoric without any proof. The GED Testing Service says, “You are scored on not just how well you can quote from the passages, but also on whether you can express your own thoughts about your chosen evidence. So you

should explain why the evidence you’ve chosen helps you make the point you want to make.” Do not over quote to fill up your essay with words! Only use quotes when needed to support your argument.

The Prompt In the GED® test, the "stimulus material" is the text, passage, or information you’ll read to understand the context of the question.

After the stimulus material, you’ll find a question, also known as the " prompt ." The prompt will ask you to respond to the material and will include specific instructions.

Screenshot of stimulus material from a GED practice test

In your response, develop an argument in which you explain how one position is better supported than the other. Incorporate relevant and specific evidence from both sources to support your argument.

Read some sample prompts to become familiar with the different types of essays.

• What is the true meaning of honesty? In your essay, determine whether or not honesty is always the best policy.

• What is one event from your life that taught you a powerful life lesson? Use your personal observations and experience to describe why that lesson was valuable.

• Who is the most important member of your family to you? Describe your relationship to this person and your reasons for selecting him or her.

• Consider how our society has changed over time. Are young people today better off than they were in the past? Write an essay explaining why or why not.

Remember, the better-argued position is not necessarily the position with which you agree. This task should take approximately 45 minutes to complete.

Sample Question Between the guidelines and the prompt, you have all the instructions you need to write a good essay. Let’s review an official sample text for the GED language arts writing test.

Later in this lesson, you will be able to write your own essay and then compare it with an example of a good extended response.

AN ANALYSIS OF DAYLIGHTS SAVING TIME (This is an official example of a sample text)

Twice a year, most Americans adjust their clocks before bedtime to prepare for Daylight Saving Time (DST). Every spring, clocks are moved ahead one hour. In the fall, they are moved back one hour, and all to maximize the benefits of the sun. DST was first implemented in the United States in 1918 to conserve resources for the war effort, though proponents encouraged its adoption long before then. Benjamin Franklin, for example, touted the idea of DST to citizens of France way back in 1784!

DST in America

For years following DST’s U.S. debut, cities could choose if and when they wanted to participate. However, by the 1960s, the open choice resulted in various cities throughout the United States using different times. These varying times created confusion, particularly for entertainment and transportation schedules. Imagine traveling across several states, each adhering to its own little time zone!

In order to remedy the confusing situation, Congress established a start and stop date for DST when it passed the Uniform Time Act of 1966. Although this act helped clarify when DST went into effect around the

country, cities were not required to use DST. To this day, parts of Arizona and all of Hawaii, for example, do not use DST.

Benefits of DST

Many studies have investigated the benefits and costs of DST. Research in the 1970s found that DST saved about 1% per day in energy costs. On average, most electricity used is for lighting and appliances. It makes sense that more sun at the end of the day meant less need for electricity. This follows right along with Ben Franklin’s argument over 200 years ago.

Supporters of DST also claim that more sunlight saves lives. Studies have indicated that traveling home from work or school in daylight is safer. Nearly three decades of research shows an 8-11% reduction in crashes involving pedestrians and a 6-10% decrease in crashes for vehicle occupants after the spring shift to DST.

Other studies reveal that, following a similar logic, DST reduces crime because people are out completing chores after their business or school day in sunlight, lessening their exposure to crimes that are more common after dark.

Arguments against DST

Opponents of DST cite other studies that disagree with these outcomes. A 2007 study in California indicated that DST had little or no effect on energy consumption that year. A three-year study of counties in Indiana showed that residents of that state spent $8.6 million more each year for energy, and air pollution increased after the state switched to DST. The researchers theorized that the energy jump was caused in part by increased use of air conditioning as a result of maximizing daylight hours.

Recent research has also brought into question the safety aspect of the yearly switch to and from DST. In one study, pedestrian fatalities from cars increased immediately after clocks were set back in the fall. Another study showed 227 pedestrians were killed in the week following the end of DST, compared with 65 pedestrians killed the week before DST ended.

The adjustment period drivers endure each year is a dangerous time for pedestrians, and Daylight Saving Time may be the reason. Instead of a gradual transition in the morning or afternoon by just minutes of sunlight each day, the immediate shift of one hour forward or backward fails to provide drivers and pedestrians time to adjust.

When you also consider the cost of the abrupt transition in terms of confusion caused by people who forget to adjust their clocks, opponents say, any benefits gained by DST are simply not worth the trouble.

Prompt:

The article presents arguments from both supporters and critics of Daylight Saving Time who disagree about the practice’s impact on energy consumption and safety.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the article to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from the article to support your response. Remember, the better-argued position is not necessarily the position with which you agree. This task should take approximately 45 minutes to complete.

Mastering the GED Extended Response Essay Before you write your essay, let’s look at what the testers are looking for in your essay. Responses to the essay questions are scored according to several qualities:

Creation of arguments and use of evidence

Your essay should have:

• a thesis directly relevant to the text and the prompt

• a good analysis of the arguments in the passage (for example, are the opposing arguments supported and believable?)

• relevant examples from the text to support your argument

Development of ideas and organizational structure

Your essay should have:

• logical, well-developed ideas

• organized ideas

• good transitions

• a formal essay structure (the one you’ve learned)

• the right words to express your ideas

Clarity and command of standard English conventions

Your essay should have:

• correct sentence structure, avoiding wordiness, run-ons, and sentence fragments

• correct capital letters, grammar, and punctuation

Explore further: Discover additional resources to deepen your understanding. The GED guidelines all give very clear directions about how to write your essay. You can use the instructions as a checklist when you practice writing essays and during your test. View and download the GED essay-writing guidelines This video will help you understand how to write your Extended Response essay for the GED® Language Arts test. Click here to watch the video You can also click here to watch an extensive video with more examples and explanations on how to write your extended response.

Practice Writing Your Essay Now practice writing an essay. You can do this on a paper, or on a computer.

At the following link, you can see an example of a sample write-up and some prompts:

Sample Write-up and Prompts

After writing your essay, you can use the example below to compare your essay with what a good extended response could look like.
